THE "AVIS." Christiansted, St. Croix. TUESDAY, 1 st JANUARY, 1856.

Tl»c Tear I H9H, The Year 1855 is now numbered among its predecessors, and forms an additional link in the continuous chain of time. It has been the practice and lime-honored custom of the periodical press to indulge in a retrospect of the past, on commencing the labours of a new year. We took up our pen with the intention to prosecute this duty, but such a catalogue of direful events crowd upon the memory as being associated with 1855 that perbe more " honored in the breach than in the haps the practice, in the present instance, would observance." But while we do hot desire to interrupt the festivities of the Season with a minute review of the melancholy disasters which have bcfalleu other Countries, some of them within this Archipelago, during the past year, we think the present a becoming opportunity to record our acknowledgments of the Divine goodness in mercifully preserving our Island from the calamities of fire, flood, teuipest, plague, <J'c., which have been abroad on the Earth, and by which so much valuable life and property have been lost and destroyed Not far from our own shores the monster Cholera is at the present moment dealing devastation þÿ the citizens of Porto Rico being the unfortunate victims. We deeply sympathize and condole with our neighbors in their affliction, and fervently pray that the hand of the destroying angel may speedily be stayed. Should we be visited by such a calamity þÿ which Heaven forbid þÿ our Island would dreadfully suffer from its effects, þÿ experience having taught

us that the scourge of which we are speaking is more severely felt among the rural or agricultural population We have the fact before us that Cholera invariably makes its first appearance in the country districts ; the mind could scarcely picture our situation in the event of such a visitation. Let us then þÿ one and all þÿ offer our gratitude to God for our undeserved protection, and humble ourselves before Him for a continuance of His mercies. Our meed of praise wc beg to tender to the Authorities of this town for their unweary exertions in warding off the pestilenoe ; may they continuo so to do.

We have also much cause of thankfulness that nothing has occurred during the past year to interrupt the internal tranquility of the Island. Other Countries have been distracted and divided with civil wars and party differences, but we have been blessed with peace. The differences which threatened a rupture between the Mother Country and the United States of America, arising out of the question of the Sound Dues, we have every confidence will soou be amicably settled. A war between the two nations would bo seriously felt by these Islands iu the interruption of the regular supply of Provisions received from the Ports of the Union.

The relations of England, France and Turkey (as Allies with Russia are at the present time interrupted with War and bloodshed; and the political horizon is very porteutious of coming events. We trust, however, in the merciful in" terposition of a kind Providence ; and hope that universal peace may soou be permanently restored. We are entering auspiciously on the commencement of a new year, and are animated witli hope as to future prosperity. We have among us a new Governor, of pleasing report, in the person of His Excellency Johan Frederik Schlegel, who, wc are glad to find, takes a lively interest in the welfare of the Colony, and who, we rejoice to say, is already gaining the affection of the community, and promises to be exceedingly popular for his courtesy, activity and zeal. With such a distinguished and influential Chief to further our exertions, and to make our true situation and wants known to the Danish Government, wo hope to obtain all the advantages to our interests. Let us, therefore, take courage, and be up and doiug, trusting to Divine Providence for His blessing on our industrious exertions.

During the past year remorseless Death entered family circles, and removed to another, and, we trust, a better world, many a beloved relative or friend. Some who were in the enjoyment of health and strength at this time last year are now the inhabitants of eternity. The call is a loud one to us to be also ready. That man lives well who lives prepared to die. May it be our study so to live ! Another year of our probationary existence has expired, and we have now entered upon the course of a new one. May the contemplation of past mercies call forth our gratitude, and may the present year abound with lasting comforts, and temporal and religious blessings to all. And, lastly, a word for ourselves ! In commencing a new Volume, wo owe it as a duty to our Patrons to thank them for their past support. This we cheerfully do. It has been our desire to render the " Avis" not only a useful periodical, but also a respectable family Journal, and if we have not succeeded to the extent of our desires, it is not because we have not striven. We have done our best to accomplish this object, and to merit public patronage. Our columns are " open to all, influenced by none" ; but, alas ! the local contributions to our paper þÿ aye, con tributions of any þÿdescription are of such a scanty nature, as to debar us the possibility of placing before the public tuauy matters of deep interest, and sometimes vital importance, which may not have come to our direct or immediate knowledge. Many there are whoso pens may

be profitably used in this way, with credit to the writer and advantage to the general community, but there is an apparent inertness prevailing here for which we cannot possibly account. Our planter-friends particularly may, now and j again, favor us with a sketch renew 1 oondition, <f-c. We again of their agricultural our labours

with this object in view, and with a determination, as far as may be in our power, to promote and advance the interests of St. Croix ; and again thanking our friends and patrons for their past support, wo cordially and sincerely wish to each and all " A Happy New Year."

marine intelligence. Wreck at Ancgatla ! The American schooner-yacht Ultra, of about 100 tons, Captain Wii.eiam N.

Lawrence, was wrecked at Anegada reefs on the morning of the 13th inst. The Ultra left New York on the 8th November bound to Pernambuco, Brazil, on a voyage of pearl-fishing. On the 10th she encountered a gale and lost her rudder. On the 15th fell in with the U. S. ship, St. Loms, which vessel remained by her during that night, and rendered every assistance in hanging a temporary rudder. From the 15th November to the 13th inst., (during which time Capt. Lawrence was endeavoring to make St. Thomas,) encountered nothing but a succession of gales. Soon after striking on the reef the Ultra sund into 8 fathoms water. Captain Lawrence had barely time to take to his boat with the crew, and could not even save his papers, logbook or chronometer. Captain Lawrence's protest is worthy of perusal, as it shews the dangers and hardships which himself and crew endured for nearly a month þÿ tossed, as they were, to and fro, on the restless sea, þÿ and the many efforts made in the way strapping ropes under her keel and lashing them up the shrouds, to preserve, if possible, her masts, one of which was ultimately carried away. þÿ Ibid.

A Remarkable Speaking Tube. þÿ A fact in acoustics has just been established at Mr. Henry Greenwood's printing establishment. Mr. Greenwood's private office is in Canning-place, his printing-office in Trafford-chambers, South John-street. The distance is about 400 feet, and on Monday a gutta percha tube, of an inch diameter, was carried through yards, houses, cellars, &c., and then passed up to the upper story of Trafford-chambers. When completed, the effect was tested with perfect success. A person speaking at one extremity in Canning-place was heard as distinctly in South John-street as if he had been within a yard of the speaker. The tube was manufactured and fixed up by Mr. S. Hellcwell, of the Quadrant, Limestreet. Some scientific gentlemen recommended a tube of a larger diameter, and one of an inch and a half was tried without success ; and the inference is, that the smaller the tube the more distinct the words conveyed. Does this suggest the possibility of a speakingtube for miles along a railway ? þÿ Liverpool Journal.

How to Drive a þÿNail. In driving a cut nail into hard wood, its entrance will be much facilitated by dipping it into oil, or what will answer nearly as well, wet it with water. Experienced carpenters are in the habit of putting a nail into the mouth to wet it, before attempting to drive it into hard wood. When a nail is to remain permanently, salt water is preferable to oil, as the former will rust the nail and cause it to take a firmer hold. In all cases it is better to insert a nail so that its widest diameter shall stand parellel with the grain of wood. This is generally done with thin boards, where there is danger of splitting, but it should always be done, even in nailing into a solid piece of timber ; for where a rupture does not take place by setting the wide part of the nail across the grain, yet a slight opening is produced near the nail, which admits air and moisture and hastens decay around it. þÿ Boston Post.

The Gumbee Troupe ! On Wednesday afternoon last their Sable Majesties the King and Queen of a country Gumbee Troupe made a triumphal entry into this town, accompanied by their retinue, and presented themselves before His Excellency. A large concourse of servants and others were present to witness this absurd exhibition of mock royalty. The Troupe were richly attired in silks and satins, þÿ the cost of which, no doubt,

was defrayed from the hard earned savings of a whole year. We doubt much the propriety of encouraging such needless extravagance on the part of the9e people. Ignorance is very apt to mistake toleration for commendation ; and being aware of the well-known characteristic of the negro, engendered through slavery þÿ we mean their improvidence þÿ we think less inducement ought to be given to them thus to squander their earnings in such senseless mockery. Where is the use of our Savings' Banks, if we uphold and encourage that class of the people, who could be most benefited by such an Institution, to waste their earnings in such ridiculous amusements ? We certainly mean to leave to each individual the right to amuse himself in the manner suited to his taste. But their are certain tastes which, although wo cannot prevent their manifestation, still are so repugnant to common sense and even to decency, that we are justified in showing our disfavor, and in endeavoring, consistently with the individual right of the parties, by all the means within our power, to suppress. The Gumbee we regard as the manifestation, par excellence, of such a taste !

The European intelligence connected with the War is not of such a nature as to afford much interest ; indeed, we cannot reasonably look for any important move on the part of the Allies before next Spring. Such items, however, as are furnished by the latest London dates we give below : þÿ CAPITULATION OF KARS. General Williams (observes the Morning Chronicle) has, at length, been obliged to capitulate. Finding himself redueed by famine to the last extremity, and having no prospect of relief, the brave Commander of Kars found it impossible to protract the siege any longer. Although overcome at last, the brave garrison of Kars has yielded to necessity, without, however, having lost any of its laurels. The proverbial endurance of the Turkish soldiers has been fully maintained, and their reputation, when properly led and handled, remains undiminished. The news of the catastrophe is brought by General Kraety, who, with another officer, has eluded the Russian cordon and escaped. The siege of Kars will always be a bright episode in the history of the war. Hastily fortified, and garrisoned by the relics of a beaten army, but guided by skilful and zealous British officers, Kars has sustained a blockade of six month and repelled two assaults. The services of General Williams, Lieut. -Colonel Lake, Major Teesdale, Capt. Thompson, Mr. Churchill, and Dr. Sandwith will uot readily be fotgotten.

The Times contains a dispatch from its Vienna correspondent, dated Dec. 13th, stating that of Kars. The Globe says : þÿ nothing was then known in that city of the fall " We fear, however, that this gives no ground for hope that the intelligence of the capitulation which has been published is otherwise than too true in svery respect."

THE WAR The Minister-at-War at Paris, received a telegraphic message from Marshal Pelissier, on Thursday : þÿ " Sebastopol, December 8. I have this moment received the following dispatch from the General commanding the first division of the first corps From 2,000 to 3,000 Foot, and from 400 to 500 Horse, attacked Baga, Orkousta and Skvaka, this morning, by daylight. The enemy beat a retreat, after a heavy fire of musketry for an hour. About 30 prisoners, two of whom are officers, have been left behind in our hands. There are also some dead and wounded, the number of whom I do not know. Our loss is insignificant." Baga, Orkousta and Skvaka arc three villages situated at the Eastern extremity of the Valley ot Baidar, and form the extreme right of the French position as well as that of the allied army. Our allies arc posted very strongly here, and their reserves are close at hand

THE ZULU - KAFIR IMFI1EE, OR "SWEET REED." Our attention lias been lately directed to a Pamphlet, printed for private circuknown author of the " Sugar Planter's lation, by Mr. Leonard Wray, the well- Companion," and of " The Practical Sugar Planter," on the " Zulu-Kafir Imphee, or Sweet Reed," in which the botanical characters, the mode of cultivation, the yield and manufacture into Sugar and other products from its rich saccharine juice, of a new. and, as Mr. Wray predicts, a successful rival of the Beet Root and Sugar Cane, are concisely, although clearly and tersely described ; and, as the subject is one of much and " go-a-headism," we have thought importance in these days of competition it right to bring the matter before our Readers and the Public, in the following short resume of Mr. Wray's Pamphlet, which is rather too long to be inserted in its entirety in our periodical. Our neighbours in Trinidad have taken up the question warmly, and Mr. Dreveton, the Secretary of the Society of Agriculture of Point-a-Pitre, in a letter to the Editor of the Trinidad Reporter, has run a tilt against a writer in Martinique, who maintains that the seed of the plant in question is only meant for Canary Birds, and states that steps have been taken in Trinidad and Martinique to cultivate the plant in order to test its capabilities. Time alone will show who " Little is right, but, in the meanwhile, we of England," who lead the van in agriculture in these latitudes, should not be behind hand in trying any experiment

which may tend to increase the comforts of our fellowmen, while at the same time it opens a new source of wealth for ourselves ; and it affords us much gratification in stating, that steps have already been taken to ensure the introduction of the plant here. Thcfirstseedof the "Imphee" brought to this Island, was given by Mr. Wray to Mr. Iligginson, (late of Joes River Estate) and was brought out by him in June, 1854. There were three varieties, but only a very small portion of each, and the melancholy state of affairs consequent on the Cholera Epidemic, retarded the planting of it for some time ; only a few stalks of the plant were grown from this seed, and being unfortunately much exposed to the ravages of birds, the grain was entirely destroyed before it ripened. On Mr. Higginson's return to England, Mr. Wray made him his Agent, sent out parcels of two varieties of seed and the necessary documents to empower him to apply on his behalf to the Legislature for an enactment to protect him in the manufacture of Sugar and other products from this novel source. A Petition to that effect was prepared by Mr. Kerr, to whom the agency was transferred, and presented to the House of Assembly, during the last Legislative Session ; and that Gentleman has since handed

over the seed sent out by Mr. Wray to Mr. Douglas, the much-respected and experienced Attorney of Mount IVilton Estate, who, we believe, ietends to bestow the necessary care upon its cultivation, and (if the seed is found sufficient) to plant two acres of land with it. Mr. Wray promises us a much larger and more comprehensive edition of his Pamphlet in a short time, in which the results of the various experiments performed in England, Belgium, and the Continent with the different varieties of the Imphee will be fully detailed. " The Imphee," according to Mr. Wray, "is the Holous Sacciiaratus of Linnaeus, Brown, and other Botanists, belonging to the Family Graminaceae, to which also the Sugar Cane, Guinea Corn, and Indian Corn belong, but is a perfectly distinct tribe of plants from, and has no relation or affinity with, the Sorghums or Guinea Corn tribe. It was introduced into Tuscany about 178(5 by Professor Pietro Arduino of Florence, but it did not succeed ; and from that time down to the present it has been lost to Europe ; old Planter as he is, Mr. Wray knew nothing of the plant until he went to Natal, an English Colony on the South-East Coast of Africa, in 1851. "There are fifteen varieties of Imphee, of each of which he has succeeded in studying the peculiarities and value, by planting the seed, watching their daily growth, testing the saccharine value of their juices, and making Sugar from all of them in large quantities. He especially recommends three of them for

those climates which have only three or four months of hot weather, viz., the Nee-a-zana, the Boom-vwa-na, and the Oom-see-a-na, (two of which will be planted at Mount Wilton). The different varities vary in height from 8 to 15 feet, and require from 3 to 5 months to arrive at maturity. The Kafirs never cultivate the plant for its grain, but only for its sweet juice which they obtain by chewing the stalk ; and the seed, while ripening, is never attacked by birds like that of the Guinea Corn. The removal of the seed head, when ripe, does not stop the plant from growing, as every " Eye," like those of the Cane, begins immediately to swell and put forth joints. "The 'Imphee' will grow in any climate in which Indian Corn will thrive, and in any country which can afford three months of hot summer weather; but it is peculiarly adapted to Tropical climates, as with good seasons it will give three or four Crops in a year. Like the Sugar Cane, it grows well in a variety of soils, but it possesses one great advantage over that plant in the perfect immunity it enjoys from the attack of white ants. It has a decideil objection to stagnant water round its roots, although it likes abundance of moisture, and docs not require large quantities of animal manures, which only tend to the formation of a luxuriant plant but do not improve its juices. SYSTEMATIC. It will add more to your convenience and comfort through life than you can now imagine. It stives time, saves temper, stives patience, and stives money. For a while it may he a little troublesome, but you will soon find that it is easier to do right than wrong; that it is easier to act by rule than without one. Be systematic in everything ; let it extend to the most minute trifles, it is not beneath you. Whitfield could not go to sleep at night, if, after retiring, he remembered that Ins gloves and riding whip were not in their usual place, where he could lay his hand on them in the dark, on any emergency ; and such are the men who leave their mark for good on the world's history. It was by his systematic habits from youth to age that Noah Webster was enabled to leave to the world his great dictionary. " Method was the presiding spirit of his life," writes Ins biographer. Systematic men are the only reliable men ; they are the men who comply with their engagements. They are minute men. The man who has nothing to do is the man who does nothing. The man of system is soon known to do all that lie engages to do ; to do it well and do it at the time promised; consequently he has his hands full. When 1 want any mechanical job done, I go to the man whom I always find busy, and I do not fail lo find the man to do that job promptly, and to the hour. And more, teach your children to he systematic. Begin with your daughters at five years of age ; give them a drawer or two for their clothing; make it a

point to go to that drawer any hour of the day and night ; and if each article is not properly arranged, give quiet and rational admonition ; if arranged well, give affectionate praise and encouragement. Remember that children, as well as grown people, will do more to retain a name than to make one. As soon as practicable, let your child have a room which shall he lis own, and treat that room as you did the drawer ; thus you will plant and cultivate a habit of systematic action, which will bless that child while young, increase the blessing when the child becomes a parent, and extend its pleasurable influences to the close of life. A single unsystematic person in a house, is a curse to any family. A wife who has her whole establishment so arranged, from cellar to attic, that she knows, on any emergency, where to go for a required article, is a treasure to any man, (my experience, reader!) while one who never knows where anything is, and when it is by accident found, is almost sure to find it crumpled, soiled, out of order, such a wife as the latter is unworthy of the name, and is a living reproach to the mother who bore her. þÿ Hall's Journal.

Sir ! þÿ I believe it is customary in all tbc West India Colonies for the people to indulge in innocent amusement, chiefly dancing, daring the season of Christmas. It is the case here, and the laboring population on these occasions display much gauderv ; they go in bands along the streets with the Gumbce. These troops dress uniformly, and have their particular badges, flags and other emblems. Their dancing-houses and tents are always tastefully decorated, and to these crowds of people, not of the ordinary class, are attracted from curiosity. The festivities, which only a few days ago passed by, were observed with mirth and decorum no riots occurring order and decency þÿ þÿ prevailing throughout the season þÿ Christmas Day being devoted to Divine service. In making these remarks I am constrained to say that it was very gratifying to notice with what courtesy the different companies were received by our popular Governor and Lady. From an early hour on New þÿYear Day s these people were to be seen wending their way towards Government House to wish His Excellency and Cousort a Happy New Year. Laborers from the country, in their gay attire, partook also of tho opportunity afforded them of expressing the compliments of the season. And it is with great pleasure I state that His þÿExcellency s unbounded courtesy actuated him to allow a troop from the country to visit him yesterday, at their express desire, being prevented from doing
in the afternoon they were seen coming along þÿKing Street, s both men and women, mounted

3 m a A T It 8, on horses, and nicely dressed. They soon put themselves in order, and amidst a dense crowd of people of all classes, who had assembled in the yard of Government House, commenced dancing, which however did not last long. They then went to the house of their employer, and after enjoying themselves there, returned quietly to their homes. This state of things promises well for the future. A little display of that sort during these festivities, which is an old custom, cannot depreciate the worth of this class of people, who, with a little encouragement and some soft solder, perhaps would do better. They like these shows, and when allowed to indulge in them at this time, seem to give more satisfaction. PUBLICOLA. Christiausted, 3rd January, 1856. To the Editor of the St. Croix þÿ Avis þÿ, Sir ! þÿPalmerston evening s organ adds seven magnificent steam-vessels to our present Baltic fleet as all ready for service in the Spring, besides the gun-boats and mortar- vessels launched every week. It sums our fleet next Spring at 40 lineof-battle ships and heavily armed frigates, 20 corvettes, and smaller vessels of war, 170 or 180 gun and mortar-boats of light draught, each mounting from one to four guns of heavy calibre. Two hundred and thirty vessels propelled by steam in the Baltic under the English pennant ! These will carry more than the usual force of Marine artillery and Marines. Under Sir W. Codringtou there will be 70,000 British, 20,000 Turkish Contingent, 10,000 or 12,000 German, Swiss and Italian legion. The men are not on paper, but in the field or near it ; and when the Globe calculates that the French and Sardinians will bring us aid enough to furnish altogether more than double our 100,000, we may freely give it credit for modesty in its estimates. Moreover, it promises energetic measures for keeping up and increasing our reserves. If, then, wc have an enemy ready for us þÿ if we have postponed preparation till there is no chance of surprise, at all events we are no longer trifling with the mightiest possible event. The contest may yet be uncertain or þÿtedious must be treirondous, but we are showing that Great Britain is in her element in such a strife, that her spirit is not quelled, her might not dwarfed. Win or lose, we take our place as of yore, among the

strongest aud the foremost. We strive for successes now, we need the peace it brings for all the aims we cherish. But sternest of all is the necessity of showing that we have not degenerated. This contest closed, we must have shown friend and foe that in years to come it will not bo safe to injure or insult us. We must conquer peace, and in so doing, give such blows as will show that it is best not again to break þÿit.

DID THE EMPEROR NICHOLAS COM- MIT SUICIDE ? At an inquiry, hold before Mr. Wakley, on Friday, into the circumstances attending the death of a person who had suffered from an affection of the pulmonary organs, the disease to which the late Emperor of þÿRussia s death was attributed, the coroner, in remarking upon the case, observed, þÿ In the case of the Emperor Nicholas, his death was put down to paralysis of the lungs and bronchitis, which, according to the symptoms described, was known by us medical men to have been impossible, and to have been stated only to deceive the public mind. The official document describing the þÿEmperor death, s stated that, at the last he took leave of his family with a firm voice, a proceeding physically impossible if he was suffering from the disease stated in the certificate of death. The belief, therefore, on the minds of the medical men in this country was, that the Emperor was poisoned; and that is my opinion, not, at the same time, that he was poisoned by those about him, but that he committed þÿsuicide.

From the Barbados Agricultural Ueporter, November 8, 1855. THE ZULU - KAFIR IMPURE, OR þÿ SWEET þÿREEl).

(Concluded.) þÿ is It propagated by seed, which it is better to soak in warm water a day or two before planting, and in temperate climates it is advisable to hatch the plants under a glass lor a month and then plant them out in the open ground. The seed may be planted with a drill and must be very lightly covered, in rows 3 feet apart with 12 inches between each drill along the rows ; but this is a point which differences in the soil, climate, season, and variety of seed used will cause to vary accordingly. An acre of land thus planted will have 14,000 Stools, each of which will produce from 5 to 20 Cents, and, at a low average, will afford 84.000 Canes weighing 63, 000 lbs. and capable of yielding at 70 per cent, (which was the per centage obtained by Mr. VVray with a common vertical wooden roller Mill made in Natal at a cost of £2) 44.000 lbs. of Juice containing 15 per cent of Sugar, which with ordinary skill will give from li to 2 Tons of good, dry, fair coloured Muscovado Sugar. The Stalks make superior Manure, which is their proper use, or serve as Fuel, the same as Cane Trash. The Leaves and long Tops ire excellent food for Stock, and the Seed, of which an acre of land, on a low average, will yield 20 bushels, may be used as grain for Poultry and Animals, or may be ground into Flour as food for Man. As soon as one Crop is taken off the ground, another immediately springs up to be ready for reaping in three months if the weather permit ; and even a third and fourth Crop may be obtained from the same

planting within a year if the Seasons are propitious. þÿ The Reaping and Manufacture of the þÿ þÿImphee into Sugar are very similar to those of the Sugar Cane. The Canes are cut when fully ripe, and ground like the Sugar Cane. Mr. Wray recommends the Juice to be passed through Strainers as it comes from the Mill, so as to separate the mechanical impurities suspended in it ; cold defecation with finely sifted Lime is practised until the liquor shews an Alkaline reaction by Turmeric or other test paper ; it is then filtered, and heated to a temperature of 160 deg. or 180 deg ; an infusion of nut gall or any other agent containing Tannic Acid is then added and a further proportionate quantity of Lime to neutralize any access of Acid,

and the Liquor is again filtered and run off into Sugar in open pans over a naked fire. Although objections may be raised to the trouble occasioned by the double defecation and filtration, yet if the system be properly carried out, and the evaporating and concentrating processes be judiciously worked, the whole of the 15 per cent, of Sugar contained in the juice may be obtained in a very pure state; and Mr. Wray states very decidedly that the Lime used on the cold raw Juice does not injure the crystalizable Sugar contained in it. " In contrasting the þÿ Imphee with its two rivals the lleet Root and Sugar Cane, the following differences are the most remarkable and worthy of notice : þÿ The Imphee. 1st. Comes to maturity in from 3 to 5 months. 2nd. Ratoons three or four times in twelve months. 3rd. Contains from 70 to 75 per cent of Juice, 15 per cent of Sugar, and less Woody Fibre even in the Ratoons, which still yield the same Juice. 4th. Will yield 25 tons of Canes per acre, and from 1J to 2 tons of Sugar every 3 or 4 months. 5th. The Sugar is equal to Cane Sugar or Refined ditto, and all can be obtained from the Juice, and the Molasses is as good as that from Cane Sugar. 6th. Is propagated by Seed, suffers no deterioration, and is cultivated much more cheaply. 7th. Is free from attacks of White Ants, and from the short period of its growth not so liable to accidents. The Sugar Cane. 1st. Comes to maturity in from 12 to 20 months. 2nd. Ratoons only once in every 12 or 16 months.

3rd. Contains from 60 to 90 per cent of Juice, 18 to 20 per cent of Sugar, but the Ratoons contain more Woody Fibre, and are less juicy at eacli cutting. 4th. Will yield from 25 to 30 tons of Canes, and from 1£ to 2£ tons of Sugar every 12 or 16 months. 5th. The Sugar varies much and much is lost during the manufacture. 6th. Is apt to degenerate, and can only be propagated by cuttings, and the Cost of cultivation is much greater. 7th. Is liable to be attacked by While Ants, and from the long period of its growth, is liable to Storms, Drought and Fire. The Beet Root. 1st. Comes to maturity in from 7 to 8 months. 2nd. Does not Ratoon. 3rd. Contains from 75 to 85 per cent of juice, and from 10 to 12 per cent (?) of Sugar. 4th. Will yield half a ton of Sugar at a reaping. 5th. The Sugar is refined, but the Molasses is very inferior. 6th. The cost of cultivation is very great, as Nursery beds have to be made before the plants are planted out. 7th. Has to undergo many peculiar mechanical and chemical processes to procure the Sugar it contains in as pure a state as possible. Such then is a description of this wonderful Plant and its products, for truly wonderful must it be, if it fulfil all that is said of it. The subject is one worthy of the consideration of the Council of the General Agricultural Society, and we hope they will take it up and appoint a practical and working Committee to watch the progress of the experiment about to be tried at Mount Wilton Estate and to make a report upon
its results.

No one in his senses can question that England will remain the first monetary power of the world, so long as her vast credit system holds out. þÿ Money þÿpower, says is Swift, and universal credit is modern money. There is, therefore, to every þÿEnglishman s eye, a fearful fascination in the rise and fall of þÿ the þÿfunds, in watching day by day, the rate of þÿ þÿconsols, ( consolidated government stocks, investments in which go to meet the usual expenses of government,) and in learning the minutest particulars of the fluctuations in þÿ the money þÿmarket. A more sensitive thermometer than these same þÿ þÿfunds, has not been invented. A cheviot ram does not forbode rain, nor a Swedish lceth curl up before frost, more instinctively, than this Ludgate hill weather-prophet utters his warnings of national disaster and bankruptcy. Wo have never, since the beginning of the war, admitted the notion that one abortive campaign could seriously affect England. We have never shared in the absurd precipitancy which betrayed its hatred rather than its judgment, in proclaiming her ruin, upon every new item of her ill-luck. Wo have never dreamt that she would fall so softly, if, indeed, she was to fall at all. We kept our eyes steadily fixed upon the tide mark of her fortune þÿ the funds þÿ and until wo saw a settled and continuous ebbing there, we could not mistake passionate ravings for positive conclusions. I he last foreign mails bring ominous tidings from London þÿ change. Returns far more alarm-

ing than those of Raglan or Simpson, are issued from the Rank of England for the month of September and the first week of October. Interest has just gone up to 5J per cent, ; (dj was the maximum paid on Government stock before the war ,) specie has gouc down in the Rank withiu six weeks, a million sterling a week ; consols which sold at 'JOJ on the 6th of September, were on the 2(>th down to S7J ! The whole world of money was in dire trepidation ; earthquake shocks were felt on every bourse of the continent ; both Russia and Franco þÿ the enemy and the ally þÿ are accused of helping on the panic, by throwing immense quantities of English secu rities upon the I .ondon market, and drawing off

$ X. © Hi h ! & A T 15 3 their value, in specie. The Rank of France alone, is charged with thus crippling the Rank of England to the amount of twenty millions of dollars in gold, obtained secretly through private channels, within five or six weeks ! This conduct on the part of France, is singularly significant, taken in connection with the notorious fact, that when that government lately opened its new loan for war purposes, the French people actually gave it twice as much as it asked. The comparative failure of the western harvests, the consequent high price of provisions, and the drainage on French specie for foreign produce, no doubt prompted the Rank of France to replenish its vaults against the coming storm ; that it has done so at a present sacrifice seems likely, but it may reasonably hope to reimburse itself in time, if it can continue to receive its ordinary amount of deposits at four per cent, interest, while at London they have to offer five and ahalf to stimulate public confidence, or rather we should say, to excite public cupidity. The money article of the London Times October 5th, talks of þÿ the strange proceedings of the Rank of France the Chronicle of the same day admits the decrease would þÿ have been greater, but that a very large amount (of specie) had been obtained in the þÿmarket þÿ we suppose from Australia and California chiefly. The London News, of October 6th, speaks of þÿ the present remarkable bullion operations of the Rank of þÿFrance, and the same paper thus explains

the modus operand i of these operations : þÿ þÿ We have to repeat, then, (says the News,) that tho first contract was for forty millions of francs, or say £1,000,000, and was taken by Messrs. K. Raphael and Sons. Forty days were allowed for the fulfilment of this contract, but it was completed within a month from its date, and the whole of the transaction was thus terminated within the last three weeks. The entire sum of £1,600,000, payable to Messrs. Raphael for this gold, was defrayed, we arc informed, by short bills on London, representing bona fuh transactions at maturity, including bank post bills and bank notes, together with some remittances in silver. In fact, the whole of this operation seems to have been carried out without accommodation paper of any description, and the real position of the matter would appear to bo that advantage was taken of every available debt due in the course of trade from England to France to facilitate the withdrawal of the £1 ,600,000 in gold from this country. It was chiefly with reference to these circumstances that we cautioned the public not to rely upon the reflux of this gold. Tho second contract was for 75,000,000 franks, or about £8,000,000, and was also offered to Messrs. Raphael <$- Sons, who, however, having a regard to the tightening tendency of tho money market, respectfully decliued it The contract for this sum was then accepted by another of the principal monetary firms of London, and is now in course of execution Wo believe

the price at which the second contract was taken is 10s. premium per milk, or 1,000 francs The premiums paid by the Rank of France is thus calculated to be at the rate of about one þÿpercent. With these facts before us the meaning of the run by one national Rank on the other becomes clearer. France can afford to pay one jie.r rent premium for bullion London, thereby in il she can continue her home operations at on. amt a half per cent, lower interest than England. In other words, if she can from the fulness of her vaults depress the rate of interest in France one and a-half per cent, under the English rate, she makes a half per cent, at least upon the bullion abstracted by hor agents from the Rank of England. It is to be sure a desperate game, but so long as it pays it will be risked by that specula live power, whose grand operations, whether in

finance or war, are generally rapid and adventu rous. We may safely infer that Napoleon 111 is at the bottom of this damaging run on his þÿAlly s treasury. With what object > The money ar tide of the Times before quoted unconsciously supplies an answer The writer, after allowing for the Turkish loan, sent in specie to Constanti nople, and half a million for breadstuff's to the Danube, observes : þÿ þÿ These modes of absorbing our surplus means being for the most part arrested, the question simply is whether the annual profits of the country from its trade, which the enemy cannot disturb, are sufficient to meet the sum to be sunk in materials of destruction, and in the pay of those who, diverted from reproductive labor, are employed in þÿdestruction. In other words, whether þÿEngland s annual gains by trade will balance her aunual losses by war. Not surely if any great power, like France, which has no deficit but a surplus in its public Treasury, should turn stock-broker on an impe rial scale, collect Rritish securities and British bank paper all over Europe, throw them cn mass' on the home market, and insist on England re deeming her paper in gold ? This is a condition of the financial problem, which the Times, not to add to the panic, has thought proper to overlook. Like the late Czar Nicholas, the new Napo Icon, seems fully to comprehend that the funded system of Europe is the golden field of modern diplomacy The same mail þÿ the Atlantic's þÿ has brought us an evidence of his activity in this

way, at Madrid, which reflects a strange light upon his contemporaneous operations at London The story is thus told by the London corrcs pondent of the Times of this city, (for whose tone the reader will allow) : þÿ þÿ The Emperor has hit upon a plan of getting the Spanish Contingent, not lacking in iugcuuity It does away the money difficulty, but it docs no more. It is, however, worthy of meutiou He has just sent two of the Directors of his faiuou clap-trap financial and political engine, called the Credit Mobihcr, to Madrid, to offer the Spanish Government a large sum, said to he $60,006,000, on condition that the said Government grant to the Credit Mobilier the right to make and opt rate the great lines of railway mentioned in a late letter, for sixty years, the money to be paid in part on the receipt of the charters, and a pari in various successive installments The naviga tiou of the river Ebro also enters into the contract, and this part of it has already been obtain cd by the Credit Mobilier This all looks vcr\ nicely, but the secret of the business is simply this : The Credit Mobilier is Louis Napoleon and a few of his instruments , the so-called Di rectors sent to Madrid are an Ex-Minister of Finance and an Ex-Chief of Police in his employ The $60,000,000 are the bait thrown to Spain to lure her into the power of the Emperor, and either get the 25,000 men or a foothold in th Peninsula and a general control of Spanish politicat home and in Cuba þÿ Mere then we have the oarne þÿpower foi the

Rank of France is also but tin. agent ol the Em peror þÿ the same power who presse. with non force upon the very heait ol' British cicdit with one hand, offering millions with the other, upon the national faith of half-bankrupt Spam Why should he who has millions to spend at Madrid be draining other millions, by private arts, mil ol London < This is a question to be cogitated, it connection with the reported recall of Lord Stratford from Constantinople, the admitted growth of French influence in the east, the cm bassy from Burmah, the Murat plots in Italy, and the many other symptoms and facts which go to show, that though England i the ally ol France in the war, they are even now, ill eon cealed enemies in diplomacy

Cholera at Porto Kico ! ! J W e have before us þÿ in the St. Thomas Times of the 28th ultimo þÿ the gloomy intelligence of the increase of Cholera at Porto Rico þÿ that fearful Epidemic have spread over four other districts of the Island, namely Fajardo, J uncos, Gurabo, and Caguas (the latter on the borders of the city) ; and much apprehension is felt that the entire Island will be scourged. The following is the language of our St. Thomas contemporary : þÿ þÿ a By despatch Boat which arrived here yesterday from Humacao, and sent hither to procure a supply of medicines, -c., we learn, with deep regret, that the cases of Cholera in Naguabo had rapidly increased, the number of victims amounting to above throe hundred. The dreadful disease had also we learn commenced to spread, and made its appearance iu Fajardo, Juncos, Gurabo and Caguas. Those acquainted with the interior of Porto Rico will know that Caguas is a town or village not distant from the Capital, San Juan, and leaves us the discouraging thought that it will ultimately reach the City. We also learn that the entire Island is panic struck, and fright, which is invariably the associate of the disease, has seized possession of the public mind Would it were in the power of this Island to render efficient succour, but we fear we can only look on in sadness, and hope a change for the better will soon conic þÿaround. Self-preservation, we arc taught, is the first law of nature ; hence it becomes us all to be guarded, in the event of Cholera visiting our

Isle, or even St. Thomas. We must say all that can be done is being done by the authorities here to avoid the entrance of that loathsome disease among us. Every sanitary measure has been brought into timely operation ; and it is the duty of every citizen to cheerfully aid in the carrying out of those precautionary measures. Those who were witness to the scenes of 1853 þÿ þÿ 54 in Saint Thomas will bear us out in our remarks. þÿ þÿ The news of Cholera continues to be of a highly distressing nature. The various hamlets and villages situated on the two high roads that lead from Naguabo to Caguas, were suffering dreadfully from Cholera, which had advanced as near to the Capital, by way of Trujillo on the right and Rio Piedras on the left, as Martin Pena, seven miles from San Juan. The panic felt at the approach of the foul disease, is, no doubt, similar to that experienced in St. Thomas, when the cry was raised in the community that þÿ Cholera was at Hull þÿ! þÿ -.norr- SCIENTIFIC INQUIRIES ON CHOLERA

The Committee appointed by the General Board of Health to make scientific inquiries in relation to the visitation of Asiatic Cholera in 1854 issued their report, which contains a great deal of very valuable information, both pathological and statistical ; and though the inquiry was confined to the metropolis of London, yet the laws by which the epidemic would seem to have

been influenced apply equally to Liverpool, or any other large town. It appears that the rate of mortality all over London was 71 in 10,000 in average conditions ; but this rate varied from 6 to 179 in different districts, according to elevation, density of population, and other conditions. In 1851 the population of the metropolis averaged 30 persons to an acre, but it varies in different localities from 2 to 290 to the acre. The mortality is found to be less influenced by the comparative density than by the elevation. In the suburban and comparatively open districts of Lewisham, Wandsworth, and Hampstead, the population being respectively 2, 4, and 5 persons to the acre, die mortality from Cholera was at the rate 22, 85, and 12 respectively to 10,000 inhabitants, the comparative immunity of Hampstead being due to the fact of its being the most elevated district within the Bills of Mortality. In the three most densely populated districts, St. Luke, Strand, and East London, the population being respectively 246, 256, and 290 to the acre, the mortality was 10, 22, and 23 to every 10,000 inhabitants. The mortality was highest in districts of intermediate density. The cholera was evidently diffused over every part of the metropolis and suburbs, but it does not appear that the great differences in the density of the population exercised any decisive influence on the intensity of its operations. This is the more remarkable as the fatality of large classes of disease

has been found to increase in a given ratio to the density of the inhabitants ; and it may be inferred from this that cholera is not, like fevers, communicable by the breath. The influence of elevation, however, is decided. The four lowest districts, Newington, Rotherhithe, St. George, and Bermondsey, on the south, are all on or below the level of the Thames at high-water ; the mortality by cholera in these districts was at the rate of 112, 165, 121, and 179 to 10,000. Hampstead, Islington, Marylebone, and St. Paneras, on the north, are at average elevations of 350, 94, 87, and 73 feet above the Thames, and the mortality in these districts was 12, 11, 17, and 10. If the 36 districts of London arc arranged in the order of their elevation, tho mortality from Cholera is found not to be invariably in each inversely as the elevation ; but by taking groups of districts together a nearly regular series is obtained. Thus, the mean mortality to 10,000 persons was 156 in the districts at or below hight-watcr mark, 91 in those under 20 feet of elevation, 44 between 20 and 40 feet, 36 between 40 and 60 feet, 23 between 60 and 80 feet, 17 between 80 and 100 feet, and 10 at 350 feet. The mortality from diarrhoea varied less at different elevations than that from cholera. At the level of the Thames the deaths from cholera were as 4 to 1 compared with those from diarrhoe ; in the elevated districts north of the Thames the mortality was equal. The results of Mr. þÿGlashier inquiry s into the effect of atmos-

pheric influencus show that the years in which cholera has prevailed have had their peculiar meteorological characters, the general tendency of which has been to render the season defective in those atmospheric changes which render the purity of the air j and that these characters are such as to prevail with greatly increased development in those low levels of London where all visitations of cholera have been most fatal. High barometic pressure, excessive night temperature, hazy air, with absence of wind, ozone, and electricity, would all appear in their most marked degrees in these low lying districts. Special examinations of the atmosphere were made by Dr. Thomson and Mr. Rainey, both chemically and microscopically, but the results throw no light upon the causes of the epidemic. No relation could be traced between the disease

s v 8 » oaa a t a 3 and the presence of fungi and their sporules in the atmosphere, as they were found in tho external air as well as in the cholera wards, and continued to be observed after the epidemic had disappeared. The condition of the water supplied by tho various companies of the metropolis, ; which was examined with the microscope by Dr. Hassall and Dr. Thomson, seems of greater importance in this consideration than the air. The water supplied by all the companies is abominable, and that derived from superficial wells is as bad, from filtration through a soil deeply impregnated with the most disgusting impurities. The use of water so full of decomposing organic matter must be very prejudicial to health, and though it cannot be regarded as the source of cholera, since it is constantly used, it has undoubtedly exercised great influence in spreading ; it. The suddenness and virulence of the outbreak in the vicinity of Golden-square can be traced to no special cause, and the committee are not disposed to consider the circumstances as at all anomalous. The district, though situated at a comparatively high level, is one of the most densely populated in London, the architecture is such as to render it almost incapable of ventilation, and the atmosphere is offensive from the effluvia of defective drains. Here are all the predisposing conditions which should expose it to a violent epidemic invasion, and the committee believe that any person conversant with the laws of disease might have predicted what befcl it.

Arrival of the Packet ! This morning at a little before 7 þÿo clockthe European mails were landed here from the schr. Vigilant. Our London dates reach till the 18th November ; but there is little or nothing connected with the War to be culled from their contents. Meagre, however, us the intelligence is, we endeavor to supply it, in part, below : þÿ From the London Weekly Dispatch. TURKISH VICTORY IN ASIA. Therapia, November 15. At noon, Omer Pacha forded the river Ingour on the 5th, at the head of 20,000 men, and defeated the Russians, computed at 10,000, including Militia, and partly entrenched. The enemy lost about 400 in killed and wounded, GO prisoners, and 3 pieces of cannon. The Turkish loss was upwards of 300. The British officers did honour to their country.

This is the first authentic news of Omer Pacha received since the tidings that he had left Soukkum Kaleh, to march on Kutais. The Ingour, which he has now forced, is the largest of the many rivers which lay, or yet lies in his route, and was in every way capable of being made a strong line of military defence. It is also the frontier line of Mingrelia, in which province one of the most completely Russianized of the Caucasian lands, the Turkish Marshal now stands with his gallant army. Six months ago it was ascertained by reconnaissances that the main body of the Russians was collected at Sugdidi, only five miles beyond the Ingour, and at that place the Times correspondent on this spot thought the first battle would take place. Omer Pacha is more than half way on the road to Kutais, and, having triumphed over the greatest natural obstacles that impeded his course, has now beaten the enemy on his own ground, against every disadvantage of position. This success, coming on so soon after the battlo of Kars, completely decides the balance of the Asiatic campaign in favor of the Turks, who, as
we see, have within a short space beaten the Russians both in offensive and defensive war:

A in e r i c a . Dates from the United Stales to the 16th ult., have been lent to us. Out of the New York Herald, we clip a few extracts. It would appear that more excitement prevails in England than in America regarding the projected rupture between the two Great Powers. Tic hare never viewed the question in a serious light, much Icm of " I lie \\ ar heeling in þÿEngland, to result in War. The Herald, under the head pertinentlv remarks : þÿ þÿ There is little or no European news l>v the Pacific,. The hostile armies are in statu qua The money market is quieter. Indeed if we ex eept the rumoured appointment of Sir W C<»l rington to the command of the British arm\ in the Crimea þÿ of which we had an inkling before þÿ the week ending simultaneously with the sailing of the Pacific front Liverpool appears tn have been quite barren of events. þÿ Of rumours, however, and excitement, there was abundance in London and all over England, on the subject of the projected star with the United States. It seems that after the steamer sailed people fell a thinking of thV West India fleet, and those articles in the Time and wrought themselves up to a tremendous pitch of uneasiness about this country Som. fr-v were evidently for cutting off the American people to a man, to punish them for their suppose-! sympathy with Russia ; but the greater portion including the chief newspaper organs, viewed th spectre of war they had conjured up wit it gravo alarm and discomfort. Tender allusions to the relationship between the Americans and the

British, touching appeals to this country not t< allow itself to be dragged into a war by reckle politicians, and affectionate reminders of the com munity of interest existing between our transatlantic neighbors and ourselves, were the staph ingredient of the newspaper articles of the week As it drew near its close, and the day for the sailing of the steamer approached, the plot thickened, and the excitement grew more intense. A telegraphic message from London made the Liverpool merchants shiver, by assert-

ing that Lord Clarendon and Mr. Buclianan bad had high words, and had parted in dudgeon. Peace was reinstated on þÿ Changeby a second message asserting that the two statesmen were positively to dine together. But the next moment the merchants again collapsed at the announcement that an interchange of paper bullets had been passing all the week between the American embassy and the Foreign office, and that a war was imminent. The steamer left at this stage of the proceedings þÿ shall we say, the farce r þÿ and wc are unfortunately unable to say how it ! ended. þÿ One thing is quite certain. The English have gone off at a tangent on this war question, and will soon see the necessity of retracing their steps. They have had visions of American hostility, and dreams of pro-Russian sympathy cn this side the water, until their ideas have become a little muddled, and they have scared themselves into an idea that we were on the verge of war, when in this country, no one whose opinion is worth hearing has the least notion of anything | of the kind. þÿ The real state of our relations with Great Britain is very different from what the London Times appears to suppose. On the one side, our neutrality laws have been broken by British officials, acting, as it seems, deliberately under the orders of their government. Our authorities have put a stop to this illegal business, and reminded the British Minister, Consuls and others, that it is not the part of a friendly Power to send

agents into the country to set the people an example of violating the laws ; with which observation our government has apparently dismissed the matter, deeming the culprits in the case sufficiently punished by exposure. There is nothing very warlike in this. þÿ Next, the British Government has sent a fleet into the West Indies, where, certainly, there appeared to be no necessity for an increase of the British squadron. Inquiry instantly springs up as to the purpose of the fleet, and in the absenco of any serious indication by the British press, several plausible conjectures arc started in this country, imputing to the British designs of interference easily reconciled with their past history. It is quite possible that no interference is intended, aud that the fleet has been sent into the West India waters merely in order to spend tho winter there, so as to be in full efficiency and readiness for work itt the spring. If this bo so, an explanation to that effect will readily allay any little irritation that the sailing of tho fleet caused here. If, on the contrary, the British Government have actually had the folly to provoke a disturbance with this country by sending a fleet to the West Indies to colonize Honduras, defend St. Thomas, or overlook Cuba, it is quite evident that they have made a mistake that will be fatal to them, but which cannot, without great mismanagement on both sides, disturb the friendly relations existing between the two countries. Whatever Lord Palmerston may aspire to, the

British people will wait, at all events until they have put an end to the Czar, and conquered Russia, before they undertake to put down this country ; and as the former events do not appear likely to occur between this and the close of the month, or even within any reasonable period of time, wc can, we think, sleep soundly, without dreams of war for the þÿpresent.

E uropea n. From the London Weekly Dispatch. We give two different versions of what may very possibly turn out to bo one action. Omar Pacha has beaten the Russians opposed to him, either in passing the Anakava or the Ingour, or both. The numbers lost in each alleged encounter are so similar as to increase the probability that we have as yet only to boast of one victory. As to the 20,000 regulars asserted in the telegraphic message to be opposed to the Pacha, wo should consider the number a great exaggeration. Mouravieff could not have brought up or sent such a force from his beaten and half-consumed army, and had there been any such muster it would long ago have found its work to do upon the coast. This is enough : that the Mushir has beaten what he found before him, and that although he can no more get directly at Mouravieff than Mouravieff can set his army against him, he may so far threaten the Russian communications, and force the Russian General to look to his retreat in time, as to save the brave defenders of

Besides, the Turks have driven their enemies out of entrenchments, a reversal of all former proceedings, which raises their character for attack to something like a level with that which they have earned in obstinate defenee, a reputation which will serve them well when they next encounter their discomfited adversary. General þÿCanrobert smission to the King of Sweden and Norway is reported in one of the Danish papers as being embarrassing to the Court. The General is evidently received by all from the Sovereign to the lowest subject with lavish honours | replied þÿ! The war against Russia would doubtless be popular ; but it cannot be forgotten that the season A report comes, by way of Paris, that Russia i most dangerous for Sweden is approaching, when an army can come before the very capital, and when the peculiar force of the Scandinavians, in their fleet and gun-boats, can be of no avail. From the carefully veiled hints in the Danish journal, as well as from a letter signed þÿ A Norþÿwegian in the Times , we arc led to suppose that Norway is looking to a federation of the three

kingdoms under one head, and that if King Oscar docs not satisfy the Norwegians in his conduct towards the Czar, they would seek the renewal of their ancient connexion with Denmark, and break off their alliance, for the supposed union is little more with the Swedes. In the interest of Europe, as well as of Scandinavia, the placing of triple crown on one head would be an event highly to be desired. The Emperor of the French, in closing the Exhibition, alludes, with his usual fulness of meaning, to the state of Europe, and especially to the duties of the hitherto neutral Powers. We imagine that his words point much more decisively to Austria and Prussia than to the small Northern kingdoms, which are hesitating, not about their disposition, but their means. He plainly invokes the sense of justice in the greater Powers, when he tells them Europe would be unanimous and say who is in the right and

them for honourable arbitration, coupled with the courage necessary to make fair judgment respect ed. And it must be these selfish avoiders of present difficulties who are warned that þÿ a policy of indifference will be followed by þÿdisaster. The words from our pen are scarcely dry upon the paper which enforce the same truth. Parties are speculating upon the recall of the French Imperial Guard from the Crimea. It can betoken no indifference to the fate of the war there ; such a supposition is mere folly ; but it may reasonably indicate that a nucleus of picked and tried soldiers will be ready for action in the North if Norway and Sweden should risk a declaration of hostilities, and send a reinforcement from France to defend their territory in the winter. Canrobert and the guard at Stockholm is no incongruous idea. A speedy and an honest peace, or a war as effectual as it can be made and as unsparing in its consequences as may happen, seems to us to be the alternative which Napoleon III. is putting before the Continent in words and in deeds, and in this manly course he may count on the support of every one who has head to appreciate and heart to follow it. European. FRANCE. From the National Intelligencer. Extract from a letter from an American Resideut in France to his Friend in Washington. þÿ Paris, October ISth, 1855. þÿ Thtr apprehensions expressed in my previous letters of a commercial and financial crisis and much general distress in Europe have been daily j gaining strength. You will note that there is a j sort of war between the two great Banks of Lon- j don and Paris, owing to the latter having drawn a very largo amount of gold from the former, j This was a forced operation ; for, when bankers J can realize even one eighth of one per cent, by 1 the transmission of gold, it flows freely between the two countries under the natural operation of exchange and commerce ; but in this instance the President of the Bank of France, who is a clever and efficient officer, by a bold and decided step, agreed to pay one per cent, for one hundred raillions of francs in gold ($20,000,000.) Every- 1 thing was adroitly managed, without a shadow of suspicion in England, until the gold was in the vaults of the Bank at Paris. So great has been the drain of specie on the Bank of France that in the short interval of one month, between two of their stated publications, it had lost 156,000, 000 of francs, upwards of $30,000,000. The The hundred millions drawn from England replenishes this loss to that extent. This certainly is alarming in a specie-paying country, where bank notes only circulate in the large cities ; for even in the manufacturing towns of twenty to forty thousand inhabitants a hank note is seldom

seen, and no note is issued by the Bank for a less sum than one hundred francs. þÿ Troops continue to go forward in large numbers to the Crimea, and they are all hurried off by Bteam-frigatcs and large British steamers, which have taken 6,000 during the last few days from Marseilles. Three large American clippers are ready t ' sail from thence full of military stores, and another entire division of troops is ready to embark. During the present month | .30,000 men and 2.500 horses will have left Toulon and Marseilles. The facility and promptness with which all this immense military force and the necessary supplies are collected and sent forward is almost incredible. In former times an expedition of 20,000 men required months for its preparation and embarkment, but now it is accomplished in as many days ; and, when the present troops have sailed, France will have sent 300,000 men and 40,000 horses to a distance nearly equal to a voyage across the Atlantio, together with all the supplies for such a vast body, and all the materiel required for their use in an 1 active campaign. There really seems to be no limit to the resources of this Empire. þÿ As a proof of the fairness of the Russian publications see the frightful loss they acknow- j ledge in the horrible assault of the 8th of September in the defence of the Malakoff and Redan ; far greater than what the Allied Generals even suspected. In these accounts of the details of the killed, wounded, missing, and hors du combat ,
they acknowledge an aggregate of nearly 20,000 men. What a carnage in two or three hours !

3 ir 0 þÿA n Besides this, the Russian official reports state that for the previous month the operations of the | siege cost them five hundred to one thousand men daily, making a total loss to the effective | force of their army in a single month of at least 1 40,000 men. From the Southampton Correspondent of the St. Thomas Tidende. General Canrobert had met with a brilliant reception at the Swedish Court. A correspondent of the Daily News, writing from Stockholm i says : þÿ þÿ to a late hour last Up night numerous groups crowned the Holmes, and other elevated situations, from whence a view of the channel, with the open sea in the distance, could be obtained, j in the hope of welcoming General Canrobert on | bis landing on Swedish soil. This morning, at an early hour, the steamer Gnuthiod, from Lubeck, was signalised, and the news flew from j mouth to mouth with suoh celerity that a very large crowd had assembled at the landing-place ! by the time the steamer had come alongside, who cheered the General vociferously on his stepping on shore. þÿ It is not only to General Canrobert, ex-Commander-in-chief of the French army in the Crimea, that this ovation is paid ; the belief is general that he comes the harbinger of war. It is thought that the moment has at length arrived when Sweden will gird on her armour in right j earnest, and be ready to take a gallant part in the good cause. I have reason for asserting that great numbers of the Swedes are in favour of taking an open and honourably active part in the war against Russia. The excitement on the i subject appears now to have reached its climax. Euthusiasm in favour of the war is not only to be found in the members of the army and navy, of all grades, but it swells the bosoms of the farmer,

the artisan, the manufacturerþÿ in fact, civilians of all classes. þÿ All eyes are, therefore, turned on the French I General who comes among us at this critioal juncture, and rumours of all sorts are in circulation, | lu the military circles the þÿp .an of next þÿyear s campaign is the general theme of conversation, i and those officers who have been in Finland and Russia aro listened to at the messtable, and in the club rooms, with the most profound attention. T i have been assured, on good authority, that a general officer, who has access to royalty, has stated to his military friends that General Canrobert has full powers from the Emperor of the French to conclude a treaty of offensive and defensive alliance with Sweden, and to sottle the needful stipulations. To show how far þÿmen s minds have become familiar with the idea of hostilities with Russia, 1 will give you a plan of operations which is circulated very extensively and discussed here. Of course, under present circumstances, I do not olaim for it any authori j 1 tative origin. It is said, then, that Sweden is to furnish an army of 60,000 men besides her fleet and 200 gunboats which, are however, to undertake operations in Finland under their own commanders, and quite independently of the allied j forces ; that the Swedish contingent is to enter Finland in the spring at throe different points

simultaneously, and in corps of nearly equal strength, about 20,000 men in each. One corps will be concentrated on our northern frontiers during the winter ; it will march by land, entering Finland by Tornea, whilst the other two corps will be sent across the gulf by water, aud lauded under cover of the fleet and the flotilla of gunboats upon two points which it would be unwise at present to further particularize. þÿ The Swedish plan even goes further, and embraces the operations of the allies in the Gulf of Finland with a force of 50,000 men, land troops, which will be quite sufficient to hold the Russians in check, and enable the Swedes to overcome all difficulties in Finland, and arrive without serious opposition at the land gates of Sweaborg and Wyborg, where they would find the allied fleets ready to co-operate with them j from the sea-board. þÿ Under these circumstances, it is not to be wondered at that not only the citizens of Stockholm, but the inhabitants of Sweden generally, | hail the arrival of General Canrobert as an event I of the greatest possible importance, and await j the result of bis mission with intense exciteþÿment.

The Austrians in the Principalities þÿ A private letter from Bucharest, dated the 3rd inst., mentions as follows: þÿ A very serious affair has just occurred here. At 2 þÿo clock yesterday the English Colonel Thier was arrested in his lodgings by the Austrian military authorities. Be was stripped of bis English uniform by them, and forced to put on the Austrian great coat. Colonel Thier bad served as lieutenant in the Austrian army, and passed over with bis company in 1849 to the Piedmontese. 1 After the war he entered the British service, and advanced in it to the rank of colonel. He was sent to Kronstadt, in Transylvania, the night that followed his arrest. Be was at Bucharest 10 or 12 days, having been sent by the English Government 1o buy horses and carts for the army. Be was duly nccrei dited to the English agents, as also to Total 8 53,011(51 I the Ottoman authorities. Colonel Thier is an Hungarian. Ten minutes after his arrest, the Consul-General of England went to the house of General Coronini to reclaim the Colonel. The General gave a brief and decided refusal. Santo Domingo. By an arrival from Santo Domingo yesterday, we have had placed in our possession a number of þÿ El Dominicaiw þÿ, of the 3rd instant. Therein we find that much excitement prevails in the Republic, owing to the apprehension of another invasion being made on their territory by the Haytiens. From the London Times. We read in the Constitutionnel : þÿ þÿ It appears that Russia intends turning to account the diplomatic movement which she has just made by recognizing the established order of things in Switzerland The following is from an eye-witness and correspondent of the Lousanne Gazette : þÿ þÿ Yesterday, October 7th, the Russian Ambassador, Baron de Krudener, the gunsmith Prelaz, and one of his workmen, embarked in the boat which plies between Yevey and Villeneuve. The object of this excursion was to make trial of the carbino invented by our fellow citizen, and of which mention has already been made at the time of the reunion of officers at Mendon. Having arrived at the plain of Villeneuvc, a distance of 4,050 feet was measured by the Ambassador himself, who took his station near the target, and followed, with the aid of a telescope, the movements of the operator, M. Prelaz. 11 out of 12 shots struck the target, which was ten feet high. The Ambassador, quite pleased with the result, returned in the evening to Vevey with the inventor. One cannot but regret that the two commissioners instructed to inquire into the matter by the Federal Government should have contented themselves with a superficial examination of this new þÿcarbine. þÿ þÿThis, says La Suisse, þÿ this invention is about to become the property of Russia, if the Federal Council does not resolutely oppose such a þÿstep. þÿ

We feel uncommon pleasure in announcing that the Reverend John McNamie has been appointed by Dr. Sraccapietra, Archbishop of Port of Spain (Trinidad), to be Rector for the Roman Catholic Church in this Parish. The Reverend gentleman is last from the Island of St. Vincent, where he had laboured successfully for a period of seventeen years. We cannot, therefore, do otherwise than congratulate the Catholic community on the arrival among them of such an affectionate and zealous Pastor. In support of this we have merely to refer to the subjoined valedictory Address presented þÿ among others þÿ to Mr. McNamie by the Inhabitants of his former field of useful labour : þÿ " Reverend Vincent, " St. and Dear Sir, Sth November, 1855. " The intelligence of your preferment to an Incumbency in Santa Cruz, we regard, on your behalf, with heartfelt gratification, as a mark of high esteem conferred upon you by your Church, which however in this Island, will be deprived, by your withdrawal, of the services of a Pastor, as eminent for a zeal untiring and devoted, without a persecuting spirit, as for his charitable virtues. " But whilst we thus offer to you, Reverend Sir, our tribute of congratulation, we cannot withhold the expression of our deep regret at your departure from a Colony, where during tho lengthened period of 17 years, the unwarying exercise of the many amiable and excellent qualities you possess, has endeared you to all classes, and drawn you to us in the bonds of friendship,

enduring " We hope that in your new sphere of duty, as sincere. and amid increased labours, your valuable life may be long preserved, and that every blessing may attend your path in the prosperous Colony to which your steps are directed. " We remain, revd. and dear Sir, " Your sincere friends and well wishers, Signed by his Honor the Chief Justice, and other Members of Council, gentlemen of the House of Assembly, Magistrates, Barristers, and many other of the most respectable Inhabitants of the Island. To the Revd. John McNamie, Catholic Minister." We are further gratified to learn that the appointment of Mr. McNamie to this Parish has been approved by the Executive Authority here.
There is a report here that Cholera has made its appearance at Porto Rico ; we, however, trust it may prove unfounded.
