From the London Times, October 25, 1855. The English Government is omitting no opportunity of reinforcing the West India squadron, and thus interposing a powerful fleet between this country and the North American Continent. This proceeding will, we doubt not, call forth from a large portion of the American press that species of mild and temperate comment in which they delight whenever the conduct of England is in question, and a little political capital is to be manufactured by making her the object of invective and depreciation. We shall be told, no doubt, of the fiendish hatred of England to Republican America, and of the insolent menace behind which she veils her insidious and treacherous designs. Without the slightest wish to reflect in any way on the press which allows itself to be made the vehicle of such statements, or upon the constituencies whose votes are found to be influenced by such calumnies, we wish to point out to the good sense and moderation of the American people the causes which have led us, even in a time of war, to increase our squadron in their seas, and may possibly lead us still further in a direction the first steps towards which we arc now most unwillingly taking. We entreat, then, the American public to believe, notwithstanding the assertions to the contrary with which they are so assiduously plied, that there is no party or body of men in this country that regards them with any other feeling than that of the utmost goodwill, or would wish for them any other fate than the enjoyment of

the utmost public freedom which is consistent with the utmost private liberty and security. We have neither the wish nor the right to intrude our opinion on that form of government which has been established in the United States ; but we have, and we claim the right, to take every reasonable precaution against that spirit oi unbridled license which the present Government ot the United States seems inclined to tolerate. At this moment North America is in profound peace with the whole world ; yet it is not the less true that in her ports arc fitting out at this moment piratical filibustering expeditions, destined to carry war and bloodshed into the domi nions of an unoffending neighbour. These ex peditions do not receive the sanction of the Amc rican Government, arc not equipped by its funds will not be conducted by its officers, þÿ but thei preparation is nevertheless well known to th President and his Administration, and receive no check from that quarter. This toleration, we arc willing to suppose, proceeds from weakucp merely, and would be exchanged for vigorous action, only that the power to act is utterly wanting. The American people are so free thai they will not be controlled by a Government of their own creating, and, though laudably eager for the preservation of their own dignity and the assertion of their own rights, cannot bring themselves to tolerate an Executive sufficiently strong to compel respect for the rights of foreign nations. It is because we see no hope of finding in
the United States a Government capable of pre-

venting its citizens from waging private war on their own account agaiust the best friends and truest allies of the great republic that we arc most unwillingly compelled, even in the midst of the great European struggle in which wo are engaged, to assume a defensive attitude, in order to trample out the first sparks of this fire, and prevent a conflagration which, if once allowed to spread, may cause incalculable misery to the human race. It is the misfortune of the American Republic that she contains within her borders so many desperate and lawless men ; it is still more her misfortune that she does not possess an organization sufficiently powerful to crush these criminal attempts. That which she caunot do wo are compelled, at least so far as the lawless enterprises directed against ourselves go, to do for her. We cannot wait patiently till these lawless emissaries of insurrection and plunder have set their feet within Her Majesty's dominions, and encountered there the resistance which is sure to overwhelm their wild and desperate schemes. We cannot wait till we are placed in the terrible dilemma of either sparing men to whom clemeucy is cruelty to the human race of which they are the enemies, or of inflicting a just punishment, which may be the means of inflaming against us the passions of the American people and leading to a disastrous and fratricidal war. We will, if it be possible, prevent the crime that otherwise it would be our duty most severely to hope punish, and this We of peace. we do in the name and in the cannot believe that those

who are now engaged in enrolling unhappy men for these desperate and criminal enterprises really contemplate the success of a descent upon Ireland, for instance, as probable, or even possible. All they can hope is that the miserable fate sure to attend such wretched adventurers may be tlie means of inflaming the public mind against England, and stirring up the passions of the people to a point which might render war inevitable. This consummation it is the duty of the American Government, if it can, to prevent, and, as it cannot, of the Government against which such attempts are aimed by all means to avert. If we can prevent these expeditions from sailing, or iutercept them in mid-ocean, we shall have done much towards averting the danger that must arise should they be carried out to their natural development. The course of action wc have adopted is bold, but for that very reason we believe it to be prudent and safe. We are fully aware of the advantage that such a proceeding gives to those ever active emissaries of discord, who are incessantly employed in every State of the Union in stirring up the feelings of the populace against this country. That which is a mere measure of self-defence against lawless force they will represent as an insult offered to the lawful Government of the country ; they will declaim, they will distort, they will exaggerate, but we must not omit to prepare against real dangers because our preparations may be honestly misunderstood or designedly misrepre-

sented. England has every wish and every interest to remain at peace with America. The immense trade which wc carry on with her, the community of language and of blood, the absence of any ground of dispute or subject of rivalry, all plead forcibly in the same direction. How strange that under such circumstances we should be driven to arm merely because it is the will of a portion of the sovereign people to make war upon us, unsupported and unapproved, but also neither prevented nor arrested by the Government ! We desire above all things a continuance of peace, but if it be the determination of any large portion of the people of the United states to force war upon us we shall know how to meet it and repel it, without relaxing for an instant our gripe on the throat of the reeling and tottering giant of the north. Hut is it for the credit of those free institutions so often vaunted as all that is wise, perfect, and liberal on the face of the earth, that a friend- 1\ and kindred nation, ardently desiring peace, should feel itself compelled to stand on the defensive, not because it has any serious dispute with the Government of this free and happy community, but because that Government is unwilling or unable to prevent its citizens from going forth to murder and to plunder in the dominions of an unoffending ally ? Arc these the garlands with which the tree of freedom ought to be adorned, þÿ are these the laurels with which the temples of the goddess should be bound ?
hnglaud has some claim to be called the nursin" a

3 IP <© 1R <0 S A T It 3 mother of freedom ; and her citizens are free because they know how to obey þÿ how to subordinate their individual wills to that law the supremacy of which constitutes the principal distinction of a civilized community.

FRANCE. PARIS, Tuesday, Oct. 23, 0 p.m. Our soldiers now occupy Kinburn, and a part of our squadron, anchored in the liman of the Dnieper, cuts off all communication by sea between Odessa, Nicholaieff, and Chersou. The Russians are thus reduced to a cruel extremity, for the ships now lying in the docks of Nicholaieff, and intended to replace the fleet of Nachimoff, ingloriously sunk in the harbour of Sebastopol, can be of no possible advantage to them. We arc now in a position to menace Cherson and Nicholaieff, the latter being the great naval and military arsenal of Russia, from which might at any moment be launched a new fleet, fully equipped for another Sinope.

Positive information has been given me that the consternation of the Russians at the rapid progress made by the allies is extreme. The probability is that one of the first consequences of tho taking of Kinburn and the expedition to the mouths of the Dnieper will be, that the eight regiments of Grenadiers and the artillery division will not dare to march from Perekop to the assistance of the Russian army in the Crimea

WE FREDERIK the SEVENTH, lly the grace of God King of Denmark, the Vandals and the Goths, Dnke of Sleswick, Iiolsteen, .Stormarn, Ditiriarsh, Lauenhorg and Oldenborg, Make known : On the report of Onr Minister of Finance, who lias laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council on a Draft of Ordinance, extending the Law of 11th of March 1851 concerning transmission by post of letters and packages to the Danish West- India Possessions, We most graciously decree : The Law of the lltli of March 1851 for the kingdom of Denmark, concerning transmission by post of letters and packets, is hereby extended to the Danish West- India Possessions, in the following manner, and withthe modifications contained in this ordinance. L The postage of letters originating in, and addressed to any place in the Danish West- India Islands shall be uniform, without regard to the distance. The present rules for exemptions from paying postage shall remain unchanged until further. 2. 1) The postage of single letters shall be 4 cents, unless post- stamps are affixed to them ; these stamps to be sold by the post- department, at the rate of 3 cents a piece for a single letter, or $2. 75 for 100 stamps. Letters weighing one Danish Lod (half an ounce) or less, shall be considered as single letters. With respect to letters weighing above one Lod, the following scale shall be employed, viz : above 1, but not exceeding 2 Lod, two rates or 2 post stamps, above 2, but not exceeding 3 Lod, three rates or

3 post stamps, above 3, but not exceeding 4 Lod, four rates or 4 post stamps, above 4, but not exceeding 5 Lod, five rates or 5 post stamps, above 5, but not exceeding 6 Lod, six rates or 6 post stamps, above 6, but not exceeding 7 Lod, seven rates or 7 post stamps, above 7, but not exceeding 8 Lod, eight rates or 8 post stamps, and so on, one rate (1 post stamp) being added for every Lod up to 32 Lod. 2) For letters marked "Recommended" or "Nil" shall be paid, besides the ordinary, an additional postage of 7 cents. If, at the request of the sender, the letter is accompanied by a written acknowledgment of the receipt of the same, to be returned with the signature of the receiver, the sender shall prepay the rate of a single letter, for the return. 3) Dead letters, to be returned on demand, and letters addressed to persons who have changed their residence, shall only be charged with the postage, that originally should have been paid. 4) Envelops enclosing letters and other articles sent by the light mail shall be charged with the same postage as letters. 3. For conveyance by the post of other articles than letters the following charges shall be paid: A. The light (letter) mail. 1) For packets in general, not exceeding 32 Lod, shall be charged as for letters. Letters of address, accompanying a packet shall be weighed, together with this, in order to calculate the postage. 2) For prepaid packets not exceeding 8 Lod, sent in cross bands or single bands, and not containing any thing written but the address, the name of the sender,

the place from where the packet is sent and the date, shall be paid : not exceeding 4 Lod, one rate or one post-stamp, above 4, not exceeding 8 Lod, two rates or two post stamps. To this class belong printed price-currents, even if the prices are added in writing and proof-sheets on which only the corrections are written.

A 'H If accompanied by a letter of address, postage shall be paid for the same, as for a letter. B. The heavy (package) mail. 1) Packages and valuables in general. The postage shall consist of : a fundamental postage of 4 cents, a postage for the weight or volume, and a postage for the value. The postage for the weight or volume and for the value shall be calculated separately, according to the following tariffs : Weight or Volume- Tariff. For transmissions by sea: between the towns of Christiansted and Frederiksted in St. Croix, between the town of St. Thomas and one of the towns in St. Croix, between the town of St. Thomas and Cruxbay in St. Johns, between Cruxbay and one of the towns in St. Croix, shall be paid : For volume less than one Danish cubic-foot, according to the weight, viz : weight not exceeding one pound, 2 cents, weight above one pound not exceeding 2 pounds, 3 cents, weight above two pounds not exceeding 3 pounds, 4 cents, and so on 1 cent for each additional pound, not exceeding 10 cents, this amount being the highest postage for weight. For volume of one Danish cubic foot, 10 cents For volume above one Danish cubic foot, 7 cents per cubic foot. If the transmission is not direct between the above mentioned places, but the route combined, the different postages for the weight on the volume shall be added together. sent by the mail. The Government may raise or lower the weight or volume tariff, of which however previous information must be given to the public. Value- Tariff. The key belonging to an article, that is locked, and to be transmitted by the mail, shall not be calculated in the weight. 2) For packets not exceeding 8 Lod, without money value, with or without letters of address, shall be paid at the rate of a double letter, and may be franked by two post stamps. 3) For documents, bonds on name and other written or printed matters, filled up by writing, shall be paid as for letters, viz : «, not not exceeding 8 Lod : exceeding 1 Lod, one rate (or one post stamp), above I Lod, not exceeding 2 Lod, two rates (or 2 post stamps), above 2 Lod, not exceeding 4 Lod, three rates (or 3 post stamps), above 4 Lod, not exceeding 8 Lod, four rates (or 4 post stamps), If letters of address accompany such packets, the postage shall be calculated according to the

Communication. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, þÿ Having had the pleasure of visiting the Examination of the Danish School in this town on Tuesday last, the 13th instant, permit me, through the medium of your paper, to offer one or two remarks thereon þÿ remarks not intended, however, as criticisms springing from a fault-finding propensity, but merely as hints which, doubt, may no bo useful. Though the Examination awakened much interest on the whole, the plan adopted in carrying out the same I have always thought very detective. For instance, the fact of the examination of the upper school being carried on in two separate apartments at the same time, and with children in the. same branches, deprives one of the opportunity of witnessing all the exercises in

3 <© Ji <3 a 3£ il V 3 the different branches taught in the school. So it was in the present case ; for during the time that a very interesting exercise on Grammar was being carried on in the girls school, the boys in the next apartment were also being examined in what, I believe, they excel þÿ namely Arithmetic. As it is expected that the children are instructed to the same extent in the leading branches, why are they not brought together, and examined in those particular branches in the same apartment ? This, I consider, would bo more agreeably interesting, and wear more the appearance of a systematic arrangement. I am happy to state that the children have made great improvement since the last Examination. The exercises being principally oral, gave a better idea of the children's knowledge ; and 1 was particularly struck with the promptness with which the boys responded to the questions on the terrestrial globe, and on Geography in þÿgeneral and to a very high degree with the girls in Grammar and History. But surpassing all, the different specimens of ornamented needlework, which graced a large table, were decidedly beautiful, and nicely executed. Lady Schlegel seemed highly pleased, and pronounced the execution very good. Indeed, her ladyship expressed her highest gratification in very flattering terms to the female teacher ; and as a general opinion, has given the preference to the Examination of the West End School. I have said nothing of the Lancasterian School, not being able to spend any time there. But I
suppose the Examination there was better or worse according to the facilities that have been placed in the power of the teachers since the last Examination. X. T. West End, November 21st, 1S55.

Cliolrra al Porto Itiro ! ! ! In our last paper we stated that a report was in pretty general circulation here that this dreadful scourge to the human family had made its appearance at I'orto Hico. Since then we have received the St. Thomas Tims , of the 17th instant, confirming the sad intelligence. Our con- temporary says : þÿ " Official information has been received here by the Spanish Consul via the Capital, that Cholera had appeared in the town of Naguabo, P. It. In eighteen hours after its first appearance fourteen cases had occurred, of which five proved fatal. A Cordon had been placed around the infected district, and all communication would cease with the interior, excepting that conducted by Government. Naguabo is an eastern port of Porto ltico, and not many leagues distant from Vieques or Crab Island, which lies to the east ; the disease in its past history shows that it travels against the wind. Crab Island is our near neighbour, and we therefore hope that a powerful examination of the small boats coming from the latter Island will be enforced, as much as said boats are liable to arrive here during the night, and may commit infinite evil before their arrival is known. We think it would be worthy the attention of this
public if a small shipment of blankets, brandy, and other articles used during Cholera, were forwarded to the diseased district, as possibly there may be a scarcity."

H liy there will be no War with America. | From the Illustrated London News, Novr. 3.

Notwithstanding the premature and ill-advised outcry that has been raised about a probable rupture between Great Britain and the United States of America, we cannot bring ourselves to believe that such a disgraceful and fratricidal event is even remotely possible The people of this country would look upon such a war with horror, þÿ unless it were absolutely forced upon them by insult unatoned and unexplained, or by positive assault on our honor or our possessions, on the part of the United States. Such insult or assault the United States have not offered ; nor is it likely they will. It would be doing our brothers an act of gratuitous injury to imagine them capable of it. Whence, then, the hubbub of the last few weeks ? The statesmen of this country committed a mistake. They sanctioned the raising of an American Legion on American soil, to fight our battles against the Czar. In carrying out this worthless and unnecessary measure, our representative in the United States infringed the municipal law of the Union. The American Government demanded satisfaction. For this it is not to be blamed, either on a point of law of national policy, of morality, or of strict justice, l'ublic opinion in the " old country" exonerates the Government of the United States from all blame in the remonstrances which, in strict discharge of its duty, it has thought proper to make ; but it would not have exonerated the English Government if it had refused explanation and redress. To its honour our Government yielded

the point immediately it was mooted ; nay more, it yielded it with dignity and good feeling, neither denying nor attempting to palliate the error. The Government of the United States might have made a casus belli out of a refusal, and would in all probability have been supported in so doing by the bulk of the American people. But no such case remains, and both nations stand as they did before ; þÿ with this simple difference, that, having presumed too much upon a kindly sympathy which did not exist, and taken a liberty with a brother which he did not approve of, the English nation has learned, in a somewhat disagreeable manner, that consanguinity does not necessarily imply friendship. We all live to learn þÿ nations as well as individuals The British people now see that there is

more sympathy between Russia and the United States than they had imagined. Extremes meet. The most stringent autocracy and the unbounded democracy in the world have sentiments and passions in common. The serfs of Russia and the negro slaves of America prove, in more senses than one, that there are bonds which unite the policy of the two great empires. Another point of sympathy is the aggressive spirit which animates their foreign relations. They are both young and ambitious. They both long to clutch the possessions of their neighbours. Mexico exists for the one as Turkey does for the other ; þÿ as a tempting morsel which makes the mouth water and the fingers itch ; þÿ " grabbed at," but never wholly possessed. The a morsel often late Czar, whose cunning was as boundless as his rapacity, was fully aware of these national predilections, and of the importance of entertaining and encouraging friendly relations with tho juvenile giant of the New World. No travellers from any European nation were so welcome in St. Petersburg as the Americans. The travelling English, who penetrated almost everywhere, did not in any extraordinary numbers find their way to the banks of the Neva ; but no American of any note ever came to Europe without thinking it imperative upon him to visit the capital of the Czar. Few, or none, of them ever returned home without scattering around them, at every step of their progress, the praises of the condescension, the ability, and the glory of Nicholas 1.

The result was a kindly feeling between Russia and the United States, which would have existed under the circumstances quite independently of the present war and the passions which it has engendered, and which was cultivated by diplomacy, and extended by the manifold and daiiy-increasing relations of commerce. But whatever may be the amount of sympathy thus created þÿ however much the Irish party in to " feed fat their ancient grudge" against Eng- the Union may attempt to foster it, and thereby land ; þÿ the sense of right and justice among the American people is too strong to permit their Government to inveut a quarrel with this country for the purpose of going to war upon it. Even if it were so, Great Britain would be prepared for the contingency. All tho astuteness in the world has not been monopolised by the crafty Muscovite or the ambitious Yankee. There have been clear-headed men in London and Paris as well as in St. Petersburg and Washington. These men have foreseen the dangers that were likely to arise from the arrogance of Ultra Democracy in the New as well as from that of Ultra Absolutism in the Old World, and have proved themselves quite competent to take measures of precaution against both. The happy alliance of Great Britain and France embraces all eventualities. While it lasts it will preserve the independence of Europe against any attack, come from what quarter of the world it may and were the statesmen of America so ill advised as, out of sheer presumption and without reasonable

ground of dispute, to meddle in our present quarrel with tho Czar, the two great allies would not shrink from the responsibility of including flic United States in the number of their enemies. But this will not be. The American people are neither led by that rabid faction of expatriated Irishmen who talk so loudly against England in the newspapers and platforms of the Union, nor by that of the lawless filibusteros and traffickers in slaves who desire, and have sworn, to counted for anything, these " blatant bullies" accomplish the annexation of Cuba. If noise would, perhaps, carry the day ; but, as the anti- Finglish party in the Union make up by bluster what they want in strength, we may safely calculate that the more they bellow the less likely they are to do harm. It is the silent dog that Belbek from that of the Tchernaya. It was nebites. The American Irish represent neither the feelings nor the judgment of the United States. Their howl is mere howl, and is as repulsive to the true American as to the true Englishman. h ilibustorism is more dangerous, because it is too much in accordance with the political necessities, and the secret as well as the avowed wishes of the great pro-slavery party, not to contain within its breast the seeds of a possible rupture with Europe on the great question of Cuba. But we do not think the danger to be imminent ; and if it were it has been fully guarded against. The Americans may rely with safety upon the famous Munro doctrine, as long as they do not, under

cover of it, attack a European State. Europe will not, and docs not desire to interfere with the natural growth and progress ol the States in their own hemisphere. If Mexico is at some future day to be annexed, this country and all others in

3 Cr Ut £/ I JL A T It 3. Europe will look upon the catastrophe in somewhat the same light in which they regard the struggle now going on in China. They will think it highly interesting, and destined at some future period to become of importance, but as one in which they have no present call to interfere. At the same time, if the States assail Spain, or any other of the Powers of Europe, and endanger by that means the stability of the European system, the Muuro doctrine will become as idle as the j breath which spoke it. American statesmen know full well that the time is not ripe for a declaration of war against Spain for the possession of Cuba. They feel that they cannot undertake anything so monstrous and so wicked. They are not strong enough. Their resources, mighty as they are, would be insufficient for the purpose. They could not with impunity so-outrago the principles of international justice. If any portion of the citizens of the United States are so rash as to make private war for tho possession of Cuba, they will speedily discover that private war is robbery, piracy, and murder þÿ offences which auy ship on tho high seas, to whatsoever nation it may belong, is bouud, if it can, to prevent and punish as a measure of police. The United States form too great, too just, too noble, too generous, too religious a nation to dare to sanction such a wrong. Were they governed by au irresponsible Czar they might, under the guidance of such a man, attempt the crime. But as a free nation they cannot do it. The attempt would array against

them not only Spain, with Fnglaod and France, but the anti-slavery States of their own Confederation. Filibusterisin may try it, and the filibusteros will be hanged; but the United States will not attempt it, for if they did they would dissolve the Union. Neither Filibusterism for Cuba, nor the hatred of the American Irish against England, nor the political sympathy existing between Russia ami the United States, nor the dispute arising out of tho enlistment of the Foreign Legion, nor any other cause, will disturb the amicable relations between Great Britain and America. Both nations know how to yield when they are in the wrong ; and he who yields has in such a case the best of the quarrel.

Agricultural, ill. Drcrcton's Letter. To the Editor of the Propagateur. Sir, þÿ Your number of the 4th August current contains an article extracted from the Martiniquais, on the Sorgho. You with reason reserve your remarks upon its conclusions, that the Sorgho was only made for Canary Birds, and you decline to chime, for the present, in the de profundis, which the writer strikes up with a chuckle on its tomb. You have understood that strict caution at least was necessary in presence of a competitor which is brought forward as likely to be more formidable than the beet root. I do not know what; Sorgho it is, which was tried in Martinique. It is no fault of mine if the real "sweet reed" (roseau sucre) has not been the object of interesting experiments, for I have caused some to be delivered to the Director of the Botanical Garden of St. Pierre, with the pamphlet which poiuts out the qualities and indicates the culture of that seed. It -appears, however, that more pressing studies had been attended to at the Garden, the book was returned to me, unread, and the seeds probably await their turn for trial. two works entitled There is a Mr. Leonard Wray, the author of " The Sugar Cane Planter " " The Planter's Companion." The former is the Manual of the English Planters þÿ and a gentleman of Guadeloupe, Mr. Tonny Lemeale, has thought it so useful that he has had it translated and printed, and has kindly and gratuitously presented it to his numerous friends iu Guadeloupe. He has added a preface, which would certainly have been inserted in all the Colonial

papers, if they did not too often keep in the shade those things they should produce to the open light of day. Mr. L. Wray has passed his life in India, in Africa, and in Jamaica. The Sugar Cane has been his constant study, and he wrote those works which attach to his name among the English Planters the stamp of authority. Now, if such a man so versed in these matters comes forward in a recent work and points out to you a more generous plant than the Cane which he so well knows þÿ if lie asserts in a tone which dispels all doubt that the bcyt root is defunct, and the cane is sure to be so, pray what whose father, I am sure, must have " cracked" will the candid writer of your article say, he many witty jokes on the beet root sugar, only fit, at most, in his time, to make indifferent salads. Well ! Mr. Editor. Mr. Wray has brought the " Imphy." or sweet reed of the Zolu Caffirs, from the colony of Natal, S. E. Coast of Africa, and it is that variety of the IIolcus Saccharatus (not known to Linnmus), which lie offers to the world as being of paramount importance. I shall quote a few of his assertions. He makes a long enumeration of the processes of the manufacture of the beetroot, and says : þÿ " The manufacture of the Imphy is, on the contrary, extremely simple þÿ the sugar produced, whether brown or white, cannot be distinguished by the most competent judges from the cane sugar of similar qualities." The beet root he says, takes from 7 to 8 months to grow. It gives per acre 30 quintals of sugar,

and but very inferior molasses. The Imphy grows in 3 or 4 months, gives 30 quintals of sugar per acre, and molasses equal both in quantity and quality to that from the Sugar Cane. Let us come now, he proceeds, to the Sugar Cane, its formidable rival.

3 A\ <8 m ATI 3 a I pass over all that we know of the carc and the length of the time, i$-c., i)-e., which the cane | requires. He goes on to say þÿ " The Imphy only takes from three to four months, according to the species, to grow to maturity." "It grows free seeds, and doesnot degenerate." " It has given from a bad hand mill, 68 per cant, of juice containing 15 per cent of sugar." " Where the cane has given 30, it has yielded 25 ; but there is the second crop 3 months after the 1st, a third one three months after the 2nd, | and finally, if the weather should remain favorable, a fourth crop almost within the twelve months." He concludes with the following sentence which I translate textually : " 1 have given sufficient proofs of the accuracy of these facts and when they will be known to the world, I ask to myself, what will become of the sugar cane ?" " Where is the planter who, in the tropical regions, will not be necessarily compelled to adopt the Imphy and abandon the cane? For although in Europe, we shall only be able to get but one crop per annum, the processes of the culture is so little costly, and the means of an improved fabrication so easy, that the competition of the cane will be impossible, and inevitably the ruin of the Planter." This is what Mr. Wray announces, and there is in it the most imminent danger for the Colonies if they do not turn their attention to the. Inipliy. But thanks to (Ion there are slill in the Colonies a few intelligent men, who gather from the past lessons for the future, and who,

when they remember the beet root tremble before the imphy. I shall not speak of some trials made in a very insufficient manner; I shall confine myself to that which took place on the 31st July last. A well known name in Martinique, is certainly that of M. 1c Comte de Chazelles. This Planter and Proprietor has honourably represented Guadeloupe as its delegate in France. He directs the finest of our Central Manufactories (Usines Centrales) and every year he introduces improvements which attest a very remarkable aptitude. Well, M. lo Comte de Chazelles, on the 31st July last, at a time when the canes were only yielding at the Grande Torre do Guadeloupe, juice at 7 deg. of the Areometer, ascertained that the juice of the Imphy marked JO J strong, nearly 11, in the midst of the rainy season, after incessant ruins. ing an " Hectare" (nearly two and a half acres M. dc Chazelles in consequence, is now plant- English ) of Imphy, which he intends to cultivate in four different ways, so as to he able to arrive at the most satisfactory mode. On two other properties, sowing of Imphy will shortly take place. Let us wait, then, Mr. Editor, for God's sake! let us not consider this novel plant, which is brought to our notice, under the patronage of so respected a name as that of Mr. Leonard Wray, as mere food for "Canary birds." Sooner or later it will be placed upon our tables for consumption. (Signed; DREVETON, Secretary of the Society of Agriculture of Point-a-Pitrc. þÿ Barbados Liberal Oct. 20. ,

Rupture between England ami Ameriea. The following striking remarks are embraced in a leader of the London Weekly Dispatch, of October 28 : þÿ " We would only call upon the true men still to exert themselves, before the name of an American becomes among us, and with all the rest of the civilized world, a herald of suspicion and aversion. Mr. President Pierce has no very loDg lease of his office. There is no fear of his

re-election. lie will fall back into utter obscurity and thorough powerlessness. If, knowing any of hostile intents against a realm at peace with the one he temporarily governs, he does not use the authority in his hands to prevent collision, brought about by crime, he is himself a criminal. We will not suppose that he will have a successor who will enter upon so disgraceful a line of policy. We will hope that the idlest and least resolved will find energy enough to come forward and prevent that. If President Pierce fails in his duty, we will trust that his countrymen will hold him answerable for his misdeeds. We will not impute any wrongdoing by anticipation ; our only anxiety is to proclaim as loudly as we can that we shall yield to none. We know of nothing that would so arouse British indignation, so unite all classes in a terrible resolve to exact retribution, as any dastardly seizing upon the present supposed opportunity. We need not remind America that she has no sailors of her own to man her fleet, if she has a fleet ready to encounter ours. We need not tell her that she is herself torn asunder in factions by the riving power of a fight for the most elemental of all rights. We know that an external war might even postpone the difference and provide for the defect But let her be quite assured that we are as ready, as resolute, as eager to assert our own. As to the sending out of more vessels, with a view, we presume, of keeping the pirates off the coasts, the tax is one that the American Govern-

ment is bound to prevent being imposed upon us. The object of our Government cannot be to sink the marauders at sea, for that would be as decisive a proceeding as hanging them on shore and upon less satisfactory evidence. Perhaps, the demonstration may be sufficient to convince the brigands that their chance of plunder is infinitely less than their chance of punishment ; and, if so, in good natured allowance for the imperfection of institutions, we may be content. But if wo were to follow the lead of our feelings, we should say, " Let the scoundrels exhibit their intents quite unmistakeably, that we may have the satisfaction and the credit of ridding the earth of them." If we proceed with a more advised circumspection, a more charitable prevision, let the honest and worthy citizens of the States receive the compliment at our hands, and do their part against a common enemy far more dangerous to them than to ourselves "

Austria is endeavouring to breed a quarrel with Sardinia, so that she may humiliato or punish the Power which has dared to become the ally of England and France, and to which Italian patriots look up with hope. The cause of the quarrel is this : þÿ Count Casan, the son of a nobleman who, in 1848, fled from Lombardy and became a Sardinian subject, entered the diplomatic service of Piedmont, and, after having been attache to the legation at Constantinople for a year, was transferred to Florence. The Tuscan Government made no objection to the appointment; and the Tuscan Premier and the Austrian minister ot Florence exchanged visiting cards with the new attache. But Count Buol stepped ther, " in his position as an Austrian arch-duke," in and asked the Grand Duke of Tuscany whehe could think of receiving in his palace a person who could not be received by his Imperial Majesty or by any Austrian minister ? The Grand Duke acted upon the hint, and his Premier at first begged and then demanded that the attache should be sent away on þÿleave a demand so unprecedented that the Sardinian Government declined compliance, though it spared no pains to bring the matter to an amicable termination. The Tuscan Government then demanded that the Sardinian minister himself should be recalled, and the natural consequence was that diplomatic relations between the two Courts ceased. Sardinia might have been contented with this state of things: but Austria will not permit her to be. Count Buol, in an interview with the Sardinian

Minister at Vienna, boldly declared that "as the rupture between the Courts of Florence and Turin had taken place in consequence of instructions sent by the Imperial Government, his Majesty the Emperor would not remain out of the question, but was determined to consider it a personal one to himself." "We shall fix a time," con- tinued Count Buol, " in which the difference ought to be made up ; it does not matter to us whether there be a Sardinian Minister at Florence or not ; but if you do not settle the dispute, his Imperial Majesty will consider it a personal affair, and take measures accordingly." The Burgher Council ! It is with feelings of pleasure we notice that the Colonial Council, in framing the new Communal Law, was fully alive to the importance of making public the Proceedings of the Burgher Council.

8 S & 0 I 21 A T II 8 We are not aware to which of the honorable members we are indebted for this regulation, which, not being found in the draft, must have been added during the discussions. " The Chairman," says the law, " shall cause " an extract " in print within 14 proceedings of the days after every Session." to be published We must, however, regret that the law allows so long a period for this publication. If it is the object, in the publication of these proceedings, to give to the community an opportunity of expressing its opinions on any subject under discussion, we think the sooner the publication is made the more likely is this object to be gained. We know, from experience, that many valuable hints on subjects debated in the Colonial Council were lost to that Body from the delay in the publication of its proceedings, which appeared before the public so long after the debate, that the report to His Majesty had already been framed before it became known what turn affairs had taken. This was the case with the very law in question. An amendment had been proposed and adopted in regard to the qualifications of a voter, making the franchise narrower than proposed in the Government draft ; but this was not publicly known for many days after the final reading of the amended draft. Where could be the use of remarks then ? We, therefore, earnestly hope that the Chairman of the Burgher Council will not forget the duty he owes to the public, by availing himself of the full period (14 days) allowed him to pre-
pare the extract of the Council's proceedings, but that he will furnish the same within a few days after each Session. We look forward with interest for the Proceedings of the First Session !

We are glad to find by a notice in our advertising columns that Government, through the Royal Treasurer, is willing to treat for the purchase of all Compensation Bonds yet undrawn. We look upon this measure as one of mutual benefit ; for it will assuredly check that wicked system of advantage-taking, which it cannot be denied has hitherto been practised beyond limit in this community by the purchasers of said Bonds, and will also ensure to buyer and seller an equitable and speedy adjustment of claims

PORTO RICO Oun accounts from Porto Rico, in connection with Cholera, are not of a very late date, nevertheless of a gloomy and sorrowful character By way of illustration we take the following small paragraph from a retrospect of the past year from the pen of our contemporary of St. Thomas. He says, speaking of Porto Rico : " We see Cholera , the worst scourge of human nature, advancing on its plantations, its towns

and cities, paralysing its sinews and carrying off about three hundred of its inhabitants per day þÿ oeooo»- We notice in the St. Thomas Tidende, of 5th instant, the arrival at that Island of Governor Hi ncks, the newly-appointed Governor-General of Barbados and the Windward Islands. His Excellency arrived in the steam -ship Curlew, but too late to proceed to Windward by the last Steamer.

Euro p e a n. A NEW RUSSIAN LOAN. The house of Mendelssohn opened subscriptions of a new Russian five per Cent, loan of 50,000,000 roubles, at 86, with but little success. A money panic has commenced in Russia. At Moscow, Nishni-Novgorod, Astrakan, and other places, bank-notes are refused. People are hiding money. In order to facilitate the payments of the Treasury and Imperial Banks of Russia, the proportion of bullion in relation to bank notes is to be diminished. The payment of the interest on the national debt may, it is feared, be stopped.

Letters from Okasaki, in the Island of Japan, state that two French frigates, belonging to the naval expedition sent to the coast of Karaschatka, took possession, in the name of the allied powers, of the Island of Urup, the centre of the Russian trade in the Kuriles archipelago, and captured there a Russian cutter, laden with a rich cargo of furs. The Russian name of the Island has been changed to that of Alliance.

THE MINISTERIAL VIEW OF PEACE TERMS. Post : þÿ We copy the following from the Morning " It is certain that no peace would be safe þÿ no negociations satisfactory þÿ which did not clearly aud unmistakeably give to us all that we have won at so much cost. We have obtained by our arms the complete control, moral and physical, of Russia. But we have yet to enforce her full submission to that control for the future ; and that submission must be guaranteed not only by solemn treaties, but by untnistakeable facts. No Sebastopol in the Black Sea þÿ no Bomarsund in the þÿBaltic must ever again threaten the integrity of neighbouring þÿstates no Russian fleet may ever again darken the Euxine, ready at any moment to bear down on Constantinople, to destroy the peace of Europe, and place its safety in jeopardy. Protectorates must be abandoned, together with all pretentions to meddle with the goods, or with the subjects, of other sovereigns Not only should the waters of the Danube be free throughout their course, but their outlets must be released from the grasp of Russia, who must bo compelled to give up the possession of the mouths of the Danube. Unless such term? as these be agreed to by Russia, lot there be no peace ; but let us in the approaching campaign use all that overwhelming force with which w«are now armed for the achievement of victory."

Really we aro quite at a stand to-day for editorial matter, nothing having transpired here since our last issue worthy to be chronicled. The Weather is fine, and the Island continues healthy ; happy are wo to state also that our Sister Island, St. þÿThomas lately infected with a few isolated cases of small-pox þÿ enjoys that blessing, as will be gladly read in þÿ paragraph of our contemporary : þÿ the following It is highly þÿ gratifying to us to be enabled to tell our þÿ neighbours that this Island is in a healthy þÿ state, and, with the blessing of Providence, hope it may continue þÿso. Under present circumstances we cannot sec the utility of a quarantine being enforced here on vessels þÿ particularly our regular traders þÿ -arriving direct from St. Thomas, and we deem the subject worthy the attention of our Health Commission. The different schooners þÿ Reserve, Vigilant, and Sthollen þÿ left this port during yesterday for St. Thomas, hut we need not hope for fresh news from Europe before the morning of the 18th ; meanwhile, we supply the residue of extracts from the files on our table.

European. The following is another interesting portion of þÿ þÿCaustic s letter to the London Weekly Dispatoh : þÿ þÿ If Austria ever intended to fight, she might have fought more cheaply and effectively within the last few months than she could at any later

time. On the fall of the Southern side of Sebastopol, she and Prussia might have appeared as dictators as far as the Czar is concerned ; they might in courtesy have been accepted as not disreputable mediators by the Western Powers it they were ready to hack their demands in arms ; but now their opportunity is past for any resolute or straightforward action. The truth is that. never raised her aspirations to resolution straightforwardness. She has never affected anything nobler than the character of a dishonest bystander in a fray, ready to pick up whatever the combitants might drop, or a hottleholder that would make no great conscience of running away with his þÿprincipal s coat and waistcoat All we have to he thankful for is that this truth is universally allowed so early in the present winter that the fudge has done no more harm than to make some gambled thousands change hands unfairly, and that the wretched trick which was played upon us last year lias no chance ol repetition in this. The great promulgator of the humbug gives it up and exposes it, and all we can desire is that wc may be disgusted by no further recourse to it in the way of imposture. Just one thing, however, we may learn from the supposed terms. It is highly advantageous, no doubt, to add to the former stipulations one forbidding for ever the fortifications of the Aland Islands, but it would he infinitely better for menaced Sweden that they should lie returned to that robbed kingdom. They are worth nothing

to either State, except as points fortified for the purposes of aggression ; and, if Sweden were reinstated in their possession, Russia could never begin the building of a new Bomarsund until she had openly entered on a war and conquered the ground on which to build it. In her own case, the navigation of the Danube, is the way in which Austria proposes to deal. She would insist that Russia should cede those parts of Bessarabia which surround the mouths of the river, so that no interference with its navigation would ever again take place without open hostilities. Austria would, by the same rule, make the Black Sea a merely commercial lake, excluding from it the ships of war of all nations, in short, though she bad only put forth ideas, she has taken excellent care that they shall he such as if entertained, shall paramountly suit her own interests ; and she would have succeeded to the very height of her hopes, if she could once have got England, France, Sardinia and Turkey to adopt these as the groundwork of all future negotiation, as the terms for which they would spend blood and treasure, while she sits quietly by, secure in the war, profiting by its very course, and certain to profit most by its resnlts. IJthese are the exact terms that ought to be fought for, Austria is, of all Powers, most hound to fight for them It is only to he hoped that her schemes are seen through, and that we may apply to her statesmen the very expressive proverb that. clever for themselves From the London I Veekltj Dispatch Although some doubt has been cast upon the statement that Kars has fallen, not an individual breathing considers the event in the slightest degree improbable, or looks upon it as anything but a natural consequence of what has loug been known. Take the fact any way, suppose that Kars had not capitulated, that the garrison had held on, and starved at its post rather than surrender, the bitter reflections of every Englishman who thinks upon the matter would scarcely be alleviated. The same thing is proved, that there has been no generalship in its highest sense anywhere ; that while the commander of the respective armies abroad have, with hardly an exception ( and Omcr Pacha is among the likeliest),

been unequal to the tactical conduct of their forces, the Ministers of War and planners of the general campaign at home, have been utterly and contemptibly deficient in the grand strategy which, by their very accession to office, they profess to afford to the allied cause. What man in his senses, holding the post of Lord Panmure, or the equivalent to it in any of the other allied countries, would have suffered Kars to be starved out - Those who know the place know that it can easily be so fortified as to resist any force we may bring to retake it for a full year. Its fall throws us back for that period. It is a real advanced post for Russian conquest iu the Asiatic dominions of Turkey. It is an equivalent, if not for our holding in Sebastopol, yet for any places we have taken, or are for a long time likely to take, in the Russian possession South of the Caucasus. It helps to strike the balance in that quarter where, of all others, England is most interested, that the account should be decidedly in our favour, where deliverance from Russian usurpation should be, if we could make it so, complete and permanent. The defence, as almost improvised on the spot, has been successful beyond hope. Not only have the British and Hungarian commanders earned almost matchless name by their skill, endurance and bravery, but the Turkish troops they led and the very inhabitants of the place, stung with the remembrance of former Russian barbarities, fought as the best veterans of Europe would have combat-

ted And wo have to console ourselves with the idea that such soldiers are struck down by the want of food, and that such citize is, if they survive the famine, are, with their wives and chidren, to be exposed again to the savagery of the same hordes, sharpened by the vengeance of having been so long and so proudly resisted. Why could nut the troops of Oracr Pacha have been released from their degrading and impotent task months before they were ? Why were they ever landed on the Chersonese at all ? Why did England guarantee the Turkish loan, if during all the time since it has been negociated, no part of the proceeds could be sent in provision and ammunition to the most heroic defenders of the Turkish empire ? Did no one in Loudon, Paris or Constantinople see what Kars tells for on the map 5 Had no one brains, leisure or energy enough to plan some attempt for that partial relief which would enable the place to hold out ? Or was it, as usual, that our Ministers were utterly unprepared for good fortune and duty nobly performrd ; and that if resistance could be made, those who won the respite must be left without i any help for foresight to make the host of it ? In England, the idea that Williams, Lake, Tccsdale and Townsend should, after all their gallant deeds, find themselves prisoners in the Russian camp will excite one common burst of anger against the hollow-hearted imbecility that has loft them to their fate. It is well that it should be so, that those who will scarcely take tho pains to

reason on the importance of the loss should feel its shame, and sympathize deeply with the immediate sufferers, the heroes of our fireside talk and ot our almost familiar affections But tho truth brought home to more considerate minds is, that wc still live under the reign of blunder, of class indolence and incompetence that while ; we are struggling to free our army from pure injustices inflicted by influences at home, the same privilege and routine arc misdirecting or neglecting the most important affairs abroad, that our system is altogether a thing of haphazard I and make-believe, saved sometimes from disgrace by the valour and genius of those whom it uses worst, but sometimes, as in this instance, only made more palpable in its disgrace by sacrificing the very men who do most to palliate its injuries

3 U\ 8 H X> J'JL A T It 3 is, Russia will not have a hero in her hands to give over as a propitiation to tricky cowardly Austria. Austria has, however, one of our servants in her dungeons, and if Colonel Turr be not set at liberty before such a step can be taken, we recommend our friends to call public meetings demanding of the Government that the sneaking Power, whose pseudo-alliance with us is nothing but a gross and pernicious cheat, be called at once to account, and, in despite of all our other tusks, compelled to yield the officer in our employ. It may appear very rash and unadvised to talk of war with Austria ; but, perhaps, such a war would solve full as many difficulties as it would create, and send all parties into the right camps before the contest is renewed which must, sooner or later, become one between irresponsible dynastic autocracy and the will and rights of the mass of þÿearth inhabitants. s While on the topic of the war, we may observe that Colonel St. Auge defends Marshal Pelissier, in the Journal des Debats , against the criticisms of the Tims , by showing that the Great Napoleon always went into winter quarters, and never voluntarily quitted them unless his adversary initiated some change. Very true. But though we deplore, of all things, the necessity in a combined command, of having even to think about, much more to examine publicly, the generalship of our allies, Colonel St. Auge forces us by his reply, to put this question : When did Napoleon I. ever go into winter quarters two months before
the weather obliged him, and give away that time to a beaten enemy, instead of brilliautly following up a success ? auctioherT

From the St. Thomas Times, January 12. Tin Hispaniola War. Our late remaks relating to the defeat of the Van-guard of the army of His Imperial Majesty Faustin I. have been confirmed by the arrival of the schooner Cecilia from Porto Plata. It appears that on the 22nd uit., tho advanced guard of the Haytian army was on its way from Petit Trou to Azua, but had hardly left the former village when the noble Duke who commanded it found the roads already in possession of the Dominicans, who, in their immediate onset, gave a striking proof to the Haytians that the þÿroads at least on the eastern part of the island þÿ were not spacious enough for two ; the Van-guard fell back on the body of the army en plcinne retraitc which, our correspondent thinks, means in plain English, in full flight ! On the same day the Haytian army came up, near 20,000 strong, and immediately the Dominican order of battle was formed. We regret, however, that we are not made acquainted with the numbers of the Dominicans, but however that may be, the firing soon became extremely warm on both sides, and after a severe struggle of three or four hours duration, the Haytian army beat a Tattoo and disappeared from the field, leaving 2,000 in killed and wounded behind. The military results also, we are informed, are very great. The Dominicans are said to have lost 700 in killed and wounded. The question now to be asked is, will His Imperial Majesty Faustin I, venture another invasion of the Dominican Republic ? and if he does, will his troops follow him to those distant parts,

where fatigue and hunger, and Kentucky rifles and Machetas are as plentiful as hockle berries i We pause for a reply. We arc in receipt of the Gaceta Oficial of the 25th ult., from which we extract the Proclamation of tho Vice-President, announcing to the Dominicans the victory achieved over the Haytians by their compatriots in arms.

European. From the London Weekly Dispatch. FRANCE. The Paris correspondent of tho Morning Chronicle says : þÿ þÿ General Canrobert, who arrived here during the night of Sunday, had a long interview on Monday with the Emperor, at whioh Count Walewski, the Minister for Foreign Affairs,

waa also present. Little of course, has yet transpired as to the whole object and result of the þÿGeneral mission, s but I hear enough to repeat with confidence that an important step has been gained, the effect of which will speedily be visible. I can also confirm what I stated a few days ago, that representations have been addressed to Russia by the German Powers of the second and third order. Without going to the extent, then, of crediting all the rumours afloat as to peace negotiations, it appears clear that the Powers concerned are seriously occupied in examining on what conditions a peace can be concluded that will be acceptable to all ; that something in that way is actually being drafted either in London or here ; and that Austria has been a mover in the matter. But it would be going too far just now to assert that Austria has forwarded to Paris and London conditions to which Russia has already given her assent, for that would be to state that a treaty of peace is at the point of being signed. After her past experience as a mediator, Austria would send no conditions to her Western allies unless she was sure they would be satisfactory ; and if she has transmitted such conditions, with the consent of Russia, the whole affair would seem to be settled, since all parties are agreed. There would then be no difficulty in Austria making the declaration which I see some of the telegraphic dispatches received here announce her to have done þÿ that if Russia did not accept an

ultimatum reduced from the proposals now sent in, her diplomatic relations with St Petersburg should cease, and that she would moreover sign that military convention with the Western Powers so often talked of. There would be neither danger nor difficulty in her making such a declaration, as she would be sur de sou fait, knowing that Russia had already consented to the proposals, or, more probably, that they altogether emanated from the þÿCzar C s abinet. A few days, or even hours, will serve to dispel the present not unnatural nor blameable secrecy enveloping the great event of the existing þÿgeneration.

Sea Bathing. þÿ On entering the water at its natural temperature a feeling of shivering, with slight oppression of the chest, and convulsive respiration, termed the shock, is experienced, whioh, however, is but momentary, and passes off on immersing the whole body and moving about freely. After the bath a greater or less dsgree of reaction ensues, indicated by a genial glow, increased redness of the surface, and a feeling of general vigour, with, in some cases, eruptions on the skin. The object of sea bathing is to induce this reaction, whence its tonic proporties ; the direct action of cold having a sedative and benumbing influence, depressing the powers of life, and when prolonged causing the blood to retire from the surface, and congesting internal organs, theroby inducing coma and subsequent death. Thus it will be obvious that the period of the cold bath should not be too much prolonged, and also with a certain degreo of vigour, and power of reaction is requisite in those to whom the cold sea bath is recommended. It is, consequently, not advisable for very weak or delicate subjects, old people or those disposed to internal congestion The first biths mostly occasion a certain degree of general lassitude, with tendency to sleep, especially after meals. Some complain of oppression in the precordial region, of headache, of a tendenoy to toothache, 4-0., an attack of which is frequently induced. The appetite increases, and constipation is frequently produced These effects, however, over afterwards subside.

Cold sea bathing acts, therefore, powerfully on the nervous systom, invigorating body and mind, and increases the activity of particular organs, especially the skin, the respiratory apparatus, the lymphatic glands and absorbents.

ECCLESIASTICAL. We have much pleasure in announcing the arrival among us of the Reverend Edwin 0. Roach, British Chaplain and Rector of the Protestant Church at St. Thomas. We are further gratified to state that the revd. gentleman's stay here will be extended to a few weeks ; and that it is his intention to preach to-morrow (Wednesday) evening in St. John's Church.

We learn from accurate information that the present Bishop of Jamaica, the Right Reverend Aubrey Spencer, D. D., has determined, in consequence of his declining health, to retire from the active duties of his Diocess. The Honorable and Reverend Regenald Courtenay has been appointed to fill the station of the former Prelate. Mr. Courtknay passed through St. Thomas, en route to England in the steamer Atrato, for consecration, and will return to the West Indies in about eight or ten weeks, þÿ when it is probable he will pay our Island a visit Dr. Spencer still retains the title of Rishop of Jamaica, and Dr. Courtenay's title will be Bishop of Kingston. From all that we learn we can indeed congratulate the Church of Jamaica in the fortunate selection of a coadjutor made by their invaluable Bishop.

Below we give insertion to that portion of President Pierce's Message to the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States, relative to Denmark and the Sound Dues. The portion regarding Great Britain will have attention in our next : þÿ SOUND DUES. In pursuance of the authority conferred by a resolution of the Senate of the United States, passed on the 3d of March last, notice was given to Denmark, on the 14th day of April, of tho intention of this government to avail itself of the stipulation of the subsiding convention of friendship, commerce and navigation between that kingdom and the U . S whereby either party might after ten years, terminate the same at the expiration of one year from the date of notice for that purpose. The considerations which led mc to call the attention of Congress to that convention, and induced tho Senate to adopt the resolution referred to, still continue in full force. The convention contains an article, which, although it does not directly engage the United States to submit to the imposition of tolls on the vessels and cargoes of Americans passing into or from the Baltic sea, during the continuance of the treaty, yet may, by possibility, be construed as implying such submission. The exaction of those tolls not being justified by any principle of international law, it became the right and the duty of tho United States to relieve themselves from the implication of engagement on the subject, so as to be perfectly free to act in such way as their

public interests and honor shall demand. I remain of the opinion that the United States ought not to submit to the payment of the Sound dues, not so much because of their amount, which is a secondary matter, but because it is in effect the recognition of the right of Denmark to treat one of the great maratime highway of nations as a close sea, and the navigation of it as a privilege for which tribute may be imposed upon those who have occasion to use it. This Government on a former occasion not unlike the present, signalized its determination to maintain the freedom of the seas and of the great natural channels of navigation. The Barbary States had for a long time coerced the payment of tribute from all nations whose ships frequented the Mediterranean. To the last demand of such payment made by them the United States, although suffering less by their depredations than many other nations, returned the explicit answer that we preferred war tribute, and thus opened the way to the relief of the commerce of the world from an ignominious tax » long submitted to by the more powerful nations of Europe

If the manner of payment of Sound Dues differ from that of the tribute formerly conceded to tho Barbary States, still their exaction by Denmark has no better foundation in right. Each was, in its origin nothing but a tax on a common natural right, extorted by those who were at that time able to obstruct the free and secure enjoyment of it, but who no longer possess that power. Denmark, while resisting our assertion of the freedom of the Baltic Sound and Belts, has indicted a readiness to make some new arrangement on the subject, and has invited the Governments interested, including the United States, to bo represented in a Convention to assemble for the purpose of receiving and considering a proposition, which she intends to submit, for the capitalization of the Sound Dues, aud the distribution of the sum to be paid as commutation among the Governments, according to the respective proportions of their maritime commerce to and from the Baltic. I have declined in behalf of the United States to accept this invitation, for the most cogent reasons. One is, that Denmark does not offer to submit to the Convention the question of her right to levy the Sound Dues. A second is, that if the Convention were allowed to take cognizance of that particular question, still it would not be competent to deal with the great international principle involved which affects the right in other cases of navigation and commercial freedom, as well as that of access to the Baltic. Above all,

by the express terms of the proposition it is contemplated that the consideration of the Sound Dues shall be commingled with and made subordinate to, a matter wholly extraneous, the balance of power among the Governments of Europe. While, however, rejecting this proposition, and insisting on the right of free transit into and from the Baltic, 1 have expressed to Denmark a willingness, on the part of the United States, to share liberally with other powers in compensating her for any advantages which commerce shall hereafter derive from expenditure made by her for the improvement and safety of the navigation of the Sound or Belts. I lay before you, herewith, sundry documents on the subject, in which my views are more fully disclosed. Should no satisfactory arrangement be soon concluded, I shall again call your attention to the subject, with recommendation of such measures as may appear to be required in order to assert and secure the rights of the United States so far as they are effected by the preten tions of Denmark.

The Packet ! By the arrival of the Vigilant this morning we are in receipt of European dates to the 2nd instant, which we have hurriedly glanced over, and make a few extracts from their contents. S W E D E N. The treaty concluded on the 21st of November, between France, England and Sweden, is as þÿfollows: By Article 1, the King of Sweden engages himself not to cede to Russia, nor to exchange with her, nor to allow her to occupy any portion of the territories belonging to the crown of Sweden and Norway. The King of Sweden and Norway engages himself, moreover, not to oede to Russia any right of pasturage, or fishing ground, or of any nature whatsoever, as well for the said territories as for the coast of Sweden and Norway, and to reject any claim Russia might raise to establish the existence of any of the above-named rights. Art. 2. In case Russia should make any proposition to the King of Sweden and Norway, or any demand with a view to obtain either the cession or exchange of to the crowns of Sweden aud any portion whatever of tho territory Norway, belonging the King of Sweden and Norway engages himself to communicate immediately such proposition to the Emperor of the French and to the Queen of England ; and their said Majesties take on their part the engagement to provide the King of Sweden and Norway with sufficient naval and military lorees to co-operate with the nival and military forces of his said Majesty, with a view ,r> resist the claims or aggressions of Russia

3 ir a m & ii ;& a t n s. The nature, the importance, and the destination of the forces in question shall, the case occurring, be decided by a common agreement between the three Powers. This treaty will place the Scandinavian kingdoms under the direct protection of an alliance with England and France. Henceforth there can be no more such political crimes as the seizure of Finland ; and the aggressive spirit of Russia will be as effectually limited in the North, as, we trust, it is hereafter to be in the South and the West of her territories.

Latest Intelligence ! The following is among the latest telegraphic despatches received : Berlin, December 28. We have learned that the publication by the Swedish Government of the treaty with France and England was received with public rejoicings. Sweden is said to have sent a circular to the German Powers explaining her reasons for concluding the treaty. The document is in terms unfriendly to Russia, and fully indicates the chance of active Swedish co-operation in the Baltic next spring. It is suspected by the partisans of Russia, that the reduction of the Austrian army, accompanied by the sale of 60,000 or 70,000 horses, is a covert way of allowing the Allies to purchase them. Throughout Germany the partisans of Russia are thoroughly alarmed at the prospect of a European coalition against the Czar. Our space and time preclude the possibility of entering further into European politics to-day.

By tli e steamer Dee, which arrived yesterday morning from Jacmel, and the Dominican Mail-schooner Matilda from Porto Plata, we have come in possession of every particular relating to the skirmish at Nayba, and the battle fought on the plains of Tome, near the town of San Juan, on the 22nd ulto. between the Dominicans and Haytians. As we stated in our last number tiie operations of the Dominicans had been completely successful ; they had beaten the Haytian army and driven it back to the frontiers ; they had for two or three days harassed the retreating columns by a guerilla warfare, which had proved more fatal than the results of the pitched battle ; they had captured a large quantity of baggage, ammunition, stores, <fcc., &c., and the military chest containing a sum of $40,000; hut as this latter was no doubt, in promissary notes, its value is little better than nominal, whilst there are writers from the place who state that this sum was in specie ; they had, besides, reduced a fortress situated near the Border, held till then by the Haytian garrison. Nor do the Dominicans seem satisfied with their success; tor we learn that they were preparing to pursue their march into the Haytian territory for the purpose of conquering a permanent peace.

His Imperial Majesty Faust in ler. was at Cape Hayti, discomfited and abandoned by his troops, and unable to return to his Capital on account of a formidable conspiracy that had been discovered against him. Our correspondent thinks that His Imperial Majesty having advanced his pawns without support, has not only- lost his castle and been checked) but that his game is up ! We also learn, by private letters, that on the receipt of the news at Port-aulus army at the south, and Emperor Prince ot the defeat of the the isolated and position of the former, cries of Viva la Republiyue had been shouted in the streets and public places, and it was supposed that a determination had arisen in the minds ot the inhabitants to resist thereafter the Imperial authority. Whether his Majesty, deserted by his followþÿers as with too much truth he is said to þÿbe can reach the north and find the army there situated willing and ready to acknowledge his sovereign rule, the various private opinions that have come to hand afford us great reason to doubt. On the other band, there are those who are led to think that if Soulouque succeeds to maintain his authority over the Northern army, lie will, in order to secure his rule, abandon his designs on St. Domingo, re-enter Port-au-Prince, institute a drum-head Court Martial, and decapitate every one who dared to deny their allegiance to him. But we fear his star has sunk beneath the horison, never again to rise !
