We have perused with much interest a pamphlet entitled þÿ Letters on the Sound-Ducs- Question þÿ We have not before seen the Question so fairly and ably treated as it is by this writer. He clearly proves that there was nothing in the former relations between the United States and Denmark to justify the hostile attitude which the former has assumed towards the latter, and the whole matter must only be viewed in the light, to use the language of the author, þÿ that the United States are great and powerful, aud therefore cannot very well be quite in the wrong in a quarrel with such a small and comparatively weak nation as þÿDenmark, and that but for this reason, the Government of the United States would most likely have brought the question before the Government of Denmark in a more friendly spirit than has been manifested. In the negotiations between the United States and Great Britain regarding the free navigation of the St. Lawrenoe the conduct of the United States was not so peremptory, and, as the author of the pamphlet observes þÿ the difference in the behaviour is curious and þÿcharacteristic. We have been informed that wc are indebted to the pen of Captain Rostov, late of the Danish Army, now residing in America, for these able and lucid remarks.

The Ini pilot; ! As announced in our last, we place before the reader to-day the following report on the Imphoe. We are indebted to the kindness of our esteemed former fellow-citizen, F. Haauensen, Esquire, now a resident of St Thomas, for the possession of the document, and to the politeness of John II. Burt, Jr., Esquire, of this place, for a translation of the same : Report OJ Count de David Beauregard, President of the Agricultural Society of Toulon , on the cultivation of the Sugar-millet ( ffo/cus Saccharolus. )

1 have the honor, gentlemen, of laying before you the result of my experiments with the Sugar-millet, lately introduced into France by Mr. de Montigny, French Consul at Shang-hai, to whose enlightened zeal she is already indebted for so many other highly valuable importations I have not been able in the course of last year to procure more than 4 litres of grains, whioh have been sown at different periods, from the middle j of February to the middle of April, on about 1 hectare of land prepared as if for the cultivation of maize, which, in regard to care and expenses, has a great deal in common with those required for the cultivation of the sugar-millet. I have placed them at 30 centimetres apart from each other, in rows between which I left a space of 75 centimetres. They were cleaned and moulded twice, and also watered up to the middle of July, when I was unfortunately deprived of the necessary supply of water. I perceived but too soon that the plant remained very long

in its stage of infancy, and that a part of my first sowings was destroyed by frost. The birds, who are very greedy after this seed, have appropriated to theras 'lves one tenth of the seed, as they have subsequ utly doue with the crop. Thus there were rnauy empty spaces, though this plant grows like corn and often gives 5 or 6 shoots and even more, but the greatest injury done to this little orop was owing to drought. Had it not been for all these adverse circumstances, I do not doubt but that it would have been much more considerable. Still I have obtained from this one hectare, 30, 000 kilogrammes of canes, st ripped of their leaves and roots, which were crushed between three cylinders of cast iron, set in motion by an hydraulic wheel, which L had constructed after those used in the Colonies for the Sugar Cane, and thus gave me 16,000 litres of liquor, that fermented satisfactorily, and, on being distilled, yielded 5|0 of pure alcohol of the best taste. I must add that 1 have every reason to believe that my Still, which was out of order, has by no means given me what it ought. This juice or liquor through the whole crop showed 5 l0 after þÿLauuoe sAreometer. When you preserve the cut canes some time previous to pressing them, you get a superior quality of sugar, but it is obvious that you thereby lose in quantity what you gain in quality. Thus, 100 fine canes, cut 15 days before, and, therefore, somewhat dried up, weighed 85 kilogrammes, and have yielded 45 litres of juice, which showed 12

according to the Areometer, whilst 200 middling and small canes were required to furnish the same weight and to yield the same quantity of liquor. I have also, gentlemen, by the obliging and intelligent assistance of Mr. Verignou, Apothecary at Hyeres, been enabled to try to effect the crystallisation of the liquor of the þÿ Holcus Sacþÿoharatus. We have hitherto not succeeded with this experiment in the course of the present year, but are in hopes of arriving at a favorable result every day ; for, having conjointly made the same experience last year on a small quantity, and, loosing all expectation of seeing any crystals forming themselves, we laid the concentrated sirop aside and did not pay any further attention to it, but were in the end most agreeably surprised by finding all the sides of the pan, in which it was contained, covered with the finest crystals, which I to-day have the pleasure of laying before you in the accompanying little phial. I would also beg of you, gentlemen, to examine and guage the Ruin I have manufactured, and which I propose to you to name þÿ Rum of the Islands of þÿHyeres ; a sample of it is also deposited in your office. Gentlemen, I would not do justice to this precious þÿ þÿholcus were I to remain silent on its merits as a grain -producing plant. This wonderful plant offers that striking peculiarity, that, far from its saccharine forces diminishing in proportion as its grain ripens, those forces on the contrary are never more powerful than when it has

arrived at its perfect maturity. Besides which, the harvest derived from it appears to me to equal that of any other corn-plant, as it amply makes up by quantity for what it in other respects might be inferior in I cannot to-day wait upon you with an exact specification of its produce, not having had the time to effect the picking of the grain, however any one of you may form a pretty just estimate of its extent by calculating from the liquor yielded the number of canes obtained, every one of which bears a bag of grains weighing at least one-tenth of 1 litre. I say, at least, for the minor, secondary spikes we see shooting from the sides of each stem, however too late to ripen, must arrive at full maturity in very warm coun-

3 mrz a t a s. tries, and thereby render this plant the most precious manna for such parts of the globe. Every single member of it can be turned to use : its þÿ The Sleaui-»liip þÿ dried leaves make an excellent fodder, and, if skilfully treated, good brooms. We hardly need i add, that its liquor gives a very fine sirop, which j our house-keepers will know best how to appre- ciate As to its utility as a corn-plant, the prac- ; pioneer of a steam communication betical experiments of one of our most enterprising colleagues, Mr. M. de Maurice, on several other species of þÿ þÿholcus entitle us to entertain the best hopes in regard to this one. And now, lastly, a word on the magass which remains after the pression. All kiuds of cattle eat it willingly, and if, under a production undertaken on a large scale, it should be fouud difficult to get the enormous abundance of magass, which a machine delivers, consumed at once, the surplus would form a quautity of food for cattle equal in weight to that of the liquor, and which must in the entire process of a crop be amply sufficient to improve the soil which produced it. How many precious qualities are concentrated in this plant, which furnishes ample food to men, j beasts and earth ! Had our good Olivier de Serres known it, he would have unquestionably bestowed upon it the epithet of þÿ Treasure of housekeeping and þÿhusbandry ! I cannot terminate this report without most strenuously engaging you, in the name of our agricultural interests, to vote publio thanks to the

Government for the interest in our agriculture evinced by the instructions given to their Agents abroad, to the Imperial Agricultural Society, who have furnished us with this precious plant, as also to Mr. de Montigny, who in so meritorious a manner has shown himself worthy of the general confidence placed in him. (Signed) Count de David Beauregard.

In the New York Journal of Commerce, of the 27th ultimo, will be found an article þÿ entirely too lengthy for our columns þÿ relating to the arrest in the port of New Ycfrk of the American steamer Northern Light , for a violation of the Neutrality Act. It appears that there were on board the steamer at the time a large number of persons without passage tickets, whose presence seemed to justify the suspicion that they were connected with the supposed managers of a military expedition to Nicaragua. The circumstance having been communicated to the President, he issued an order to Capt. Bigelow of the Navy, directing the immediate seizure of the Northern Light. The authorities were opposed, when the steamer left her wharf, and proceeded down the bay with the U. S. Deputy Marshals on board, intending to take them to sea ; but when the shipping of the harbor had been well cleared, a blank cartridge was fired at her from the Revenue cutter. This was unheeded, when immediately a shot was sent, which struck the water a few feet in front of the steamer, þÿ whereupon an order was given to shut off steam, and she returned, and cast anchor in the river, near to the pier from which she started. The measures taken by the President had the effect to break up the expedition ; and the vessel was again at liberty to proceed to sea, without the men belonging to the expedition, and without military equipments.

From the St. Thomas Times , January 19. þÿTennessee. Our readers will lie pleased fo learn the arrival at this port of the United States Mail Steam-ship Tennessee, the

tween New York and Venezuela, touching tit St. Thomas and Porto itico. The Tennessee is 1,200 tons and 450 horse power, and is considered tolerably fast ; judging her sea-going qualities, and means of accommodation, by the testimonial presented Captain Johnson by his late passengers, we must conclude her to lie a safe and comfortable vessel. It is the general opinion of her passengers that in regular weather she will prove herself a five day boat between this place or St. þÿJohn (Porto s Rico) and New York. It is said that the Company, which has entered into the enterprise, is now in search of a sister ship to purchase, and that in about one month there will be two vessels on the line performing regular semi-monthly voyages between ports in North and South America. We are told the United States Government will subsidize the Company with $15,000 per annum for each vessel placed on the line, for which they are to convey a mail. Among the passengers by the Tennessee, we notice the name of Mr. Raasloff. This gentleman, we are told, comes to this island at the desire of, and by an engagement with our Government, to execute some Submarine blasting. Mr. Raasloff, it would seem, has been extensively engaged in the United States in blowing rocks at the mouths of harbours, and in the beds of rivers, and we learn has, in all cases, been successful. The rock, we presume, to be blasted here, is the one opposite the mouth of our harbour, laid down in Lieut. Lawþÿrence surveying s chart as the Scorpion
rock.

Cholera In Porto Rico ! Our advices from Arecibo are to the 15th inst., and are the most afflicting that have yet reached us from the island of Porto Rico ; they inform us that all business was entirely suspended, and that Cholera was mowing down its victims with extraordinary severity, and without discriminating between black or white, rich or poor, rural or metropolitan. Arecibo, is situated in a very low valley called on that account the Bajuras, with a broad river, the Utuado, running through it, which þÿirrigates and not unfrequently þÿinundates the whole plain witli its 24 or 25 sugar plantations established on its low banks. The Bajuras is protected from the sea by a long sandy bank, on which the town of Arecibo, is built. The whole population is about 13,000, of whom about 3,500 are slaves. To the low and swampy situation of that district, we suppose, is to lie attributed the dreadful ravages of the plague, which has cut off so large a number of inhabitants, that it was impossible to make an accurate estimate of the deaths; amongst them we very deeply deplore the loss of the þÿtraveller s friend, Don M ANUEt. Oltiz, of Ulanga Oltiz <fc Co., whose urbanity of manners and kind by our citizens; þÿ hospitality caused him to a be few well known only days before his death he saw his aged fatherin-law, and then his own youthful son, carried to the grave whither he himself was so soon to be þÿborne. llrid.

II a v a n a. From the New York Herald, January 5.J The news from Havana contains some items of interest. A report prevailed on the 25th in that city that an American vessel filled with Nicaraguan emigrants had been captured by a Spanish man-of-war, and taken into Cienfuegos. This intelligence had caused a good deal of excitement. Several important political arrests had been made in Havana, including, amongst other parties, Don Justo Poso, Don Francisco Pala. mino, Don Francisco Delgado, Doctor Ruz, and the þÿ major þÿdomo of General Concha. The prisoners were shipped off on the following day for Spain, where they are to be put upon their trial. Various rumours are assigned for this proceeding. One version of the grounds is, that a passenger on the Crescent City brought a letter to General Concha from a Cuban in Yew York, informing him that Senor Goicourria, of the Cuban Junta, was about to leave this city with 600 filibusters for the purpose of invading the island ; that they were to be reinforced on their arrival by every patriotic Cuban, and that on the landing of the expedition M. Delgado was to relieve his Excellency the Captain General of his gubernatorial functions. Another story is, that the parties whose names aro given above were overheard by a Spanish spy at the funeral ceremony in honor of General Tacon, indulging in some exceedingly bitter remarks on the dead hero, with equally flattering reflections on his successors. One, it is reported, even went the length of saying that he wished the threatened
expedition from the States would take place at onoe, so as to relieve them from such a set of scoundrels

The United Staten and the Sound Dues ! þÿ The letter addressed by the Foreign Minister of the United States to the Danish Governþÿment, says the London Picture Times of the 29th ultimo, þÿ in reply to the invitation of the latter to attend a congress upon the subject of the Sound Dues, is in more than one respect a very remarkable document ; asserting principles, which, if carried out to the fullest extent, may seriously affect the future relations of the þÿworld. After remarking on the manner in which the United States treat the claims to these dues, the same paper adds the following language : þÿ þÿ But the United States Government is not content with stopping away from the proposed convention, upon the ground of its incompetence to treat of the real question at issue between it and the Government of Denmark. Mr. Marcy in his letter goes almost out of his way to assert an additional point of principle, not altogether new, we must remark, in American policy and American pretensions, namely, a claim on the part of the New World to be altogether absolved from any concern, even by implication, in the polioy of the Old. Mr Marcy writes thus: þÿ þÿ There is another ground of objection to joining in the proposed convention. The Government of the United States will never consent to the pretension that the New World is to be appropriated to adjust the political balance of the Old It is clearly stated in the proposition which Denmark has submitted to the United States that the convention is to act upon the question relative to the Sound Dues in con-

nection with the system of the European balance of power. It is more than iutimated that the former is to be subordinated to the latter. Of the utility or wisdom of the political theory of the balance of power, in its application to the European family of nations, it is not proposed to express an opinion ; but enough of its operations has been seen to impress upon this Government a fixed determination to avoid being brought within its þÿvortex It has long been the cherished policy of this Government to avoid such a dangerous complicity ; and the President will not yield in any case to the slightest relaxation of þÿit. þÿ We have here a very large and intricate question propounded, and not very graciously, þÿ a question which the force of future events only will probably bo able to decide. We will not enlarge upon it at present ; but will simply observe, that as the whole world, Old and New, owns but one Creator, so have its inhabitants in both hemispheres interests and duties in common, which no conceits of puffed-up egotistic sufficiency can annul or supercede. With her young ambition America may consider that she can do very well without the assistance, either material or moral, of the parent States which formed and peopled her, and that she will prosper best by turning her back upon old family ties. But it was not always so The Independence of which she boasts at this day was obtained through the assistance of an old European State, was consented to in obedience to the requirements of

European policy ; and to this day her principal wealth consists in her exports of natural produce to the þÿ old þÿcountry, as her strength lies in the immigration of the sons of labour, whom circumstances induce to abandon their homes in search of employment and food. Whilst such ties as these bind the New World to þÿ the European family þÿnations, of does it not savour of pre sumption pretend to to ignore all sympathy in their interests, all care for their mutual relations ? We believe we should add, that, as a corollary to this extraordinary doctrine, tho United States pretend that the nations of tho Old World have no right to interpose in the affairs of the New World to prevent aggression or wrong to existing interests. But this is an assumption which, should the occasion arise, the Government ol the United States will find the parent States are not disposed to acquiesce in þÿ
